We collect 3,000 human demonstrations for atomic fine-tuning and will release both the demonstration data and evaluation rollout data to support reproducible real-world evaluation. Policies are fine-tuned on atomic tasks and evaluated on both atomic skill acquisition and held-out compositional tasks. We further introduce Atomic Score (AS) and Compositional Failure Share (CFS) to distinguish failures caused by weak atomic skills from failures caused by limited compositional reuse. Through 2,700 physical rollouts on five representative manipulation policies, we find that current policies can acquire simple instruction-grounding skills, but still struggle with fine-grained motor atoms, counting, and logical filtering. More importantly, strong atomic performance does not reliably transfer to held-out compositional tasks. ATOM-Bench provides a diagnostic testbed for studying whether failures arise from weak motor execution, poor instruction grounding, or limited compositional reuse.
PaperID: 91,   Spotlight  OpenReview  
Authors:  Zihao Deng, Qianhuang Li, Maggie Wigness, John G. Rogers III, Donghyun Kim, Hao Zhang
Title: Collaborative Planning for UAV-UGV Teams under Operational Constraints via Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion
Keywords: Task and motion planning, Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Planning, Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion
Abstract:
Collaborative planning under operational constraints is essential for heterogeneous robot teams in large-scale missions. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) provide rapid area coverage but are limited by onboard energy, while Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) can serve as mobile recharging stations yet are constrained by road-network traversability. Effective collaboration must enforce operational constraints during execution while enabling parallel, coordinated actions. Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have shown promise through token unmasking but have two key limitations: entropy-guided scheduling assumes distributional alignment and reliance on differentiable constraints for diffusion-time optimization. We propose Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion (MEND), which formulates collaborative planning as a conditional masked generative process to generate context-aware action sequences for UAV-UGV teams. MEND introduces a neuro-symbolic diffusion paradigm that constrains conditional masked diffusion policies at execution by reweighting the learned action distribution with a logic-induced admissibility indicator, thereby enforcing compliance with operational constraints. MEND introduces an error-bounded inference scheduling at execution that constructs the unmasking schedule by selecting positions with minimal predictive entropy over the constraint-aware action distribution, enhancing collaborative planning optimality under operational constraints. Extensive experimental results in simulation, on real-world maps, and with physical robot teams demonstrate that MEND advances UAV-UGV collaborative planning under operational constraints.
PaperID: 92,   Spotlight  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.12299    
Authors:  Hyun Joe Jeong, Gokul Swamy, Andrea Bajcsy
Title: Learning What to Say to Your VLA: Mostly Harmless Vision Language Action Model Steering
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction, Vision-language-action models, Policy Steering
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide a natural language interface to robot control, but the mapping from language to behavior is often brittle and unintuitive: semantically similar instructions can induce drastically different behaviors, while some capabilities may not be elicitable through prompting alone. As a result, both human instructions and zero-shot language models can fail to reliably steer VLAs toward successful task execution. In this work, we propose a framework that interactively searches for language sequences that improve closed-loop VLA task performance, distills these sequences into a test-time language feedback policy (LFP), and learns an improvement head that predicts when language steering will improve performance. Crucially, our approach operates on arbitrary frozen pre-trained VLAs, requiring neither access to the original training distribution nor fine-tuning of the underlying model. We conformalize this improvement head to prevent harmful steering interventions, where the LFP decreases task performance relative to the original instruction on out-of-distribution scenarios. On seen environments, our conformalized LFP improves base VLA performance by 24.7% in simulation and 65.0% in hardware. Our conformalized LFP has strong harmlessness guarantees under visual and semantic perturbations and produces recovery behaviors not observed with open-loop prompting.
PaperID: 93,   Spotlight  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.01402    
Authors:  Carlota Parés Morlans, Nils Kuhn, Y. Isabel Liu, Alberta Longhini, Jeannette Bohg
Title: Demystifying When and Why VLAs Fail in Contact-Rich Tasks and How to Fix Them
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, contact-rich manipulation, vision-language-action models
Abstract:
We address the problem of understanding when and why Vision-Language-Action models struggle with contact-rich manipulation tasks that require precise physical interaction. Prior work has primarily focused on addressing contact failures through force-augmented architectures and training-time regularizers, yet the root causes of these failures remain underexplored. We identify two distinct failure modes underlying this gap. Precision failures are rooted in a flow-matching policy training mismatch, and force failures arise from the distinctive structure of force signals. We address each failure mode with a targeted mechanism and combine them into FACT, which achieves 66% average success rate across five contact-rich tasks against 41% for the best prior baseline, in an evaluation spanning almost 2,500 real-world rollouts.
PaperID: 94,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.18933     GitHub
Authors:  Yihuai Gao, Jinyun Liu, Shuang Li, Shuran Song
Title: Gated Memory Policy
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Robot manipulation, Robot Memory
Abstract:
Robotic manipulation tasks exhibit varying memory requirements, ranging from Markovian tasks that require no memory to non-Markovian tasks that depend on historical information spanning single or multiple interaction trials. Surprisingly, simply extending observation histories of a visuomotor policy often leads to a significant performance drop due to distribution shift and overfitting. To address these issues, we propose Gated Memory Policy (GMP), a visuomotor policy that learns both when to recall memory and what to recall. To learn when to recall memory, GMP employs a learned memory gate mechanism that selectively activates history context only when necessary, improving robustness and reactivity. To learn what to recall efficiently, GMP introduces a lightweight cross-attention module that constructs effective latent memory representations. To further enhance robustness, GMP injects diffusion noise into historical actions, mitigating sensitivity to noisy or inaccurate histories during both training and inference. GMP achieves a 30.1% average success rate improvement over long-history baselines on our proposed non-Markovian benchmark MemMimic, a 26.6% improvement over VLA baselines on MIKASA-Robo benchmark, while maintaining competitive performance on Markovian tasks in RoboMimic. All code, data and in-the-wild deployment instructions will be released.
PaperID: 95,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Weirui Ye, Yen-Jen Wang, Elvis Hsieh, Zhiyang Dou, Shibo Zhao, Pieter Abbeel, Yilun Du, Leslie Pack Kaelbling, Tomás Lozano-Pérez
Title: Energy-Based Policy Orchestration
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as \emphpolicy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy--goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop \emphEPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy--goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision--robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Videos are available on the anonymous project website: \urlhttps://keen-naiad-620edc.netlify.app/.
PaperID: 96,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.09148    
Authors:  Chuanruo Ning, Tianrui Wang, Wei-Chiu Ma, Kuan Fang
Title: Proxy Policy Steering
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Policy Steering
Abstract:
Robotics foundation models carry broad manipulation priors from large-scale data, but specializing them to a new task remains the deployment bottleneck. This requires injecting new task-specific behavior from limited demonstrations without eroding their broad capabilities. We introduce Proxy Policy Steering (PPS), a novel adaptation method that addresses this challenge by training two lightweight proxy policies. A reference proxy models the frozen base's behavior on target-task observations, and a task proxy, initialized from the reference, captures how this behavior changes under task supervision. Their difference forms a calibrated velocity-space residual that steers the frozen base sampler at every denoising step. We identify the conditions under which this residual isolates the change induced by task supervision, and validate them empirically. On 8 real-world and 4 simulation manipulation tasks, PPS lifts the state-of-the-art \pi_0.5 base policy by 53% absolute success rate on average, with 0-to-1 gains on tasks the base never solves, while preserving the base's broad capabilities. PPS outperforms LoRA fine-tuning, from-scratch specialists, residual policies, and prior inference-time steering methods.
PaperID: 97,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Jianxin Bi, QIANG WANG, Jayaram Reddy, Lin Kelvin, Soibkhon Khajikhanov, Ruihan Gao, Harold Soh
Title: Heterogeneous Tactile Transformer
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Tactile Perception, Contact-Rich Manipulation
Abstract:
Tactile sensors are inherently heterogeneous: a model trained on one sensor cannot be directly used on another, which limits learning contact-rich manipulation policies from diverse tactile data at scale. To bridge this gap, we propose the Heterogeneous Tactile Transformer (HTT), a framework that learns shared tactile representations across heterogeneous sensors. HTT consists of sensor-specific encoders and a shared transformer trunk, and is pretrained with per-modality masked reconstruction together with cross-modal alignment between paired sensors. Pretraining uses our novel Heterogeneous Paired Tactile (HPT) dataset, containing 1.6M synchronized paired frames across four vision- and array-based tactile sensors. Across distinct tactile perception and real-world manipulation tasks, HTT is shown to learn transferable representations that adapt to new tasks and previously unseen sensors. Dataset, code, and model checkpoints will be released upon publication.
PaperID: 98,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Puhao Li, Zeyuan Chen, Yingying Wu, Pengkun Wei, Yuyang Li, Tianyu Wang, Jiaxiao Shi, Mingrui Yu, Baoxiong Jia, Song-Chun Zhu, Tengyu Liu, Siyuan Huang
Title: Towards Human-level Dexterous Teleoperation
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Sim-to-real transfer, Dexterous teleoperation
Abstract:
Humans routinely wield tools, swap grasps, and reposition objects within a single hand—seamlessly orchestrating contact transitions that span translation, re-orientation, and finger gaiting. Endowing robot dexterous hands with this level of in-hand dexterity through teleoperation requires precise control of object motion via dynamic hand–object contact, yet current teleoperation systems remain far from this capability. To bridge this gap, we take a major step towards human-level dexterous teleoperation by introducing TeleDexter, a hand-object co-tracking controller that maps operator intent into learned, low-level contact execution. The controller is trained on consecutive co-tracking subgoals derived from human reference motions, utilizing a hybrid reward that couples sparse subgoal objectives with dense tracking rewards to enable learning across diverse interaction modalities rather than frame-wise trajectory imitation. The entire pipeline requires only single-stage RL and, with random action masking and domain randomization, transfers zero-shot to the real robot. We evaluate TeleDexter on seven challenging dexterous teleoperation tasks spanning object reorientation and long-horizon tool use across two dexterous hands, achieving a 75% average success rate where all baselines consistently fail. Furthermore, the collected demonstrations successfully train autonomous policies via behavioral cloning, marking a concrete step towards human-level dexterous teleoperation.
PaperID: 99,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.17055    
Authors:  Dantong Niu, Zhuoyang Liu, Zekai Wang, Boning Shao, Zhao-Heng Yin, Anirudh Pai, Yuvan Sharma, Stefano Saravalle, Ruijie Zheng, Jing Wang, Ryan Punamiya, Mengda Xu, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Letian Fu, Konstantinos Kallidromitis, Matteo Gioia, Junyi Zhang, Jiaxin Ge, Haiwen Feng, Fabio Galasso, Wei Zhan, David M. Chan, Yutong Bai, Roei Herzig, Jiahui Lei, Li Fei-Fei, Ken Goldberg, Jitendra Malik, Pieter Abbeel, Yuke Zhu, Danfei Xu, Linxi Fan, Trevor Darrell
Title: T-Rex: Tactile-Reactive Dexterous Manipulation
Keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Tactile, Dexterous Manipulation
Abstract:
The ability to react dynamically to tactile signals has long been considered crucial to agile human-level dexterity. Yet contemporary learning-based VLAs for robotic manipulation generally either overlook the tactile modality or are limited to encoders with static cues, in part due to the scarcity of diverse training data and standardized evaluation, architectural constraints in current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, and limitations of static tactile encoders. In this paper, we push the frontier of tactile-reactive manipulation addressing all of these limitations. We open-source a large-scale, 100-hour tactile-rich dataset collected via a novel, data-efficient recipe that prioritizes elementary motor primitives. To effectively exploit naturally high-frequency touch signals without sacrificing the existing capabilities of existing VLAs, we introduce a variable-rate Mix-of-Transformer (MoT) architecture equipped with a novel temporal tactile VQ-VAE encoder. We demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile-reactive policies on 12 manipulation tasks requiring delicate force control, deformable object manipulation, achieving over 30% higher average success rate than the strongest baseline.
PaperID: 100,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Soumojit Bhattacharya, Oliver Kroemer, Shubham Tulsiani
Title: CS-Pi: Constraint-Satisying Flow Policy Sampling
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Flow matching policies, VLA
Abstract:
A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint that was absent from its demonstrations, such as a collision-free path or a particular grasp orientation. Existing training-free samplers take one of two approaches. \emphGuidance steers the denoising trajectory with a constraint gradient at noisy intermediates: the gradient at a noisy sample need not point toward a clean feasible one. \emphProjection maps the finished sample onto the feasible set and executes it: it is efficient, but the result is an action the policy would never draw. We find that this dichotomy need not hold. Our key insight is that the projection is a cheap, clean, feasible signal, and the only mistake is executing it. We introduce Constraint-Satisfying Flow Policy Sampling \textttCS-Pi: we draw from the policy, project the clean sample to the nearest feasible point, and resample from the flow model biased toward that point. Iterating drives the samples toward constraint satisfaction with no noisy-state gradient and no auxiliary network; the method extends to arbitrary costs with a single tweak in the projection function. We evaluate on a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, and a zero-shot Franka deployment. In every setting, \textttCS-Pi stays closest to the policy while satisfying the constraint, and it attains the highest safe-success on a real-world obstacle avoidance task.
PaperID: 101,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.13355    
Authors:  Sangkyu Lee, Seohyeon Park, Tackgeun You, Avi Caciularu, Idan Szpektor, Hwasup Lim, Youngjae Yu
Title: Real-Time Execution with Autoregressive Policies
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Real-time execution, Vision-Language-Action Model
Abstract:
Real-time execution, enabled by asynchronous inference that ensures both smooth action trajectories and fast reactivity, is critical for realistic deployments of large-scale Vision-Language-Action models. However, recent work on real-time execution primarily focuses on variants of diffusion policies, even though it is more critical for autoregressive policies given their slower rollout speed in synchronous inference. In contrast, we demonstrate that autoregressive policies can achieve real-time execution by adjusting the tokenization horizon and applying constrained decoding, thereby guaranteeing strict latency bounds that enable multi-trajectory decoding to maximize performance. Across simulated and real-world environments, we find that the autoregressive policy consistently outperforms its equivalent-level flow-matching policy counterpart while achieving significantly improved task completion speeds from synchronous inference. Coupled with the inherent advantages of autoregressive policies, such as faster convergence and better generalizability in instruction-following, these results confirm that autoregressive policies can remain a competitive policy type supporting real-time execution.
PaperID: 102,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.19425    
Authors:  Dijie Zhu, Seunghun Oh, Ruopeng Huang, Zhiyu Huang, Jiaqi Ma, Chen Tang
Title: SCAPE: Scenario-Conditioned Simulation-Augmented Policy Evaluation
Keywords: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming, Autonomous driving and flight, Robot navigation and locomotion
Abstract:
Reliable performance evaluation is a central bottleneck for deploying robot-learning policies in real-world conditions. Real-world testing produces faithful evaluation but is costly and difficult to scale, whereas simulation-based testing is easy to scale but inevitably biased due to the sim-to-real gap. Neither source alone is sufficient for scalable and reliable policy evaluation. This motivates simulation-augmented policy evaluation, which combines limited real-world rollouts with abundant simulation proxies for sample-efficient performance estimation. Yet, existing methods focus on estimating performance averaged over initial conditions and deployment settings. By construction, such population-level averages collapse scenario-specific variation, providing limited information about when and where a policy can be safely deployed. To address this limitation, we propose SCAPE, a scenario-conditioned simulation-augmented policy evaluation framework that instead predicts scenario-conditioned real-world policy performance from limited paired sim-and-real evaluation samples and large-scale simulation-based testing rollouts. SCAPE corrects the sim-to-real bias in the simulation labels before using them to train the prediction model, and calibrates the prediction uncertainty through conformal prediction. We validate SCAPE on two embodied task domains, autonomous driving and quadruped velocity tracking. In sim-to-sim settings, it reduces the scenario-level performance prediction error by 4.9%/34.7% in driving and 14.5%/27.7% in quadruped velocity tracking relative to scene-conditioned neural baselines and aggregate statistical baselines on average. We also validate SCAPE for evaluating a velocity-tracking policy deployed on a physical Unitree Go2. In addition, SCAPE improves testing sample-efficiency, produces narrower calibrated prediction intervals, enhances generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios, and unlocks fine-grained deployment strategies.
PaperID: 103,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.12498    
Authors:  Yang Yang, Tengyu Liu, Puhao Li, Zeyuan Chen, Yuyang Li, Xingwan Wang, Yingying Wu, Zhaopeng Cui, Siyuan Huang
Title: ArtManip: Category-Level Articulated In-Hand Manipulation
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Sim-to-real transfer, In-Hand Manipulation
Abstract:
Category-level in-hand manipulation of articulated objects is a formidable yet underexplored challenge for dexterous robotic hands. This difficulty stems from two core bottlenecks: first, controlling an object’s internal degrees of freedom is tightly coupled with maintaining grasp stability on a free-floating base; second, acquiring diverse object models and functional grasps at scale is highly labor-intensive, yet vital for generalization given the system’s sensitivity to initial configurations. In this work, we present our method, the first category-level articulated in-hand manipulation method that generalizes across object instances and diverse initial grasps. For initial configuration construction, we develop an automated pipeline that procedurally generates diverse articulated objects and synthesizes task-oriented functional grasps. For policy learning, we propose a robust two-stage training strategy that incorporates articulation physics randomization, reward curriculum, and latent representation distillation to handle complex contact and joint dynamics during deployment. Extensive experiments across four object categories demonstrate that our policy generalizes to unseen instances and varied configurations in simulation, and achieves zero-shot transfer to 12 real-world objects featuring diverse shapes and joint mechanics.
PaperID: 104,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.01126    
Authors:  Yuhang Lin, Jiyuan Shi, Dewei Wang, Jipeng Kong, Yong Liu, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
Title: Pro-HOI: Perceptive Root-guided Humanoid-Object Interaction
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Reinforcement learning for physical robot control
Abstract:
Executing reliable Humanoid-Object Interaction (HOI) tasks for humanoid robots is hindered by the lack of generalized control interfaces and robust closed-loop perception mechanisms. In this work, we introduce Perceptive Root-guided Humanoid-Object Interaction, Pro-HOI, a generalizable framework for robust humanoid loco-manipulation. First, we collect box-carrying motions that are suitable for real-world deployment and optimize penetration artifacts through a Signed Distance Field loss. Second, we propose a novel training framework that conditions the policy on a desired root-trajectory while utilizing reference motion exclusively as a reward. This design not only eliminates the need for intricate reward tuning but also establishes root trajectory as a universal interface for high-level planners, enabling simultaneous navigation and loco-manipulation. Furthermore, to ensure operational reliability, we incorporate a persistent object estimation module. By fusing real-time detection with Digital Twin, this module allows the robot to autonomously detect slippage and trigger re-grasping maneuvers. Empirical validation on a Unitree G1 robot demonstrates that Pro-HOI significantly outperforms baselines in generalization and robustness, achieving reliable long-horizon execution in complex real-world scenarios
PaperID: 105,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.14585    
Authors:  Hongzhan Yu, Chenghao Li, Ruipeng Zhang, Henrik I Christensen, Sicun Gao
Title: Sensitivity Shaping for Latent Modeling
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems
Abstract:
Generative dynamics models enable planning in challenging robotic systems, but safe deployment requires reliably detecting policy-induced out-of-distribution (OOD) transitions. Existing methods typically treat the learned dynamics as fixed and attach post hoc support surrogates. We show that these surrogates can fail when the dynamics are locally insensitive to critical action choices: unsupported control actions may produce latent predictions that resemble demonstrated transitions, suppressing OOD signals despite large true predictive errors. To address this, we introduce support-conditioned control-sensitivity regularization, which promotes sensitive local response to control input changes in learned dynamics in high-support training regions. This preserves control-induced variation while limiting unstable extrapolation due to weak empirical support. Experiments in vision-based obstacle avoidance, manipulation, and real-robot navigation show improved OOD detection and safer closed-loop planning.
PaperID: 106,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.40134    
Authors:  Klemens Iten, Alexander Proshkin, Bhavya Sukhija, Stelian Coros, Andreas Krause, Pieter Abbeel, Carmelo Sferrazza
Title: Tactile Curiosity Drives Robot Interaction
Keywords: Probabilistic learning and uncertainty in robotics, Tactile sensing, Exploration
Abstract:
Mastering robot manipulation skills via reinforcement learning (RL) remains largely sample-inefficient. The most common RL algorithms rely on random action sampling to discover new strategies, resulting in agents that allocate most of their training budget to motions in free space, away from the contacts from which manipulation skills emerge. Existing intrinsic motivation methods based on model disagreement or epistemic uncertainty improve on isotropic noise, but they mostly drive the agent to remain curious about functionally irrelevant transitions, such as erratic motions and interactions. In this work, we argue that tactile feedback provides a natural signal for exploration, and introduce TacEx, a framework that incorporates touch into epistemic uncertainty-driven exploration by decomposing model uncertainty across sensory modalities and directing curiosity toward the tactile channel. By anchoring curiosity to the sense of touch, TacEx drives the robot to discover complex contact dynamics, learning to manipulate and grasp objects without prior knowledge or external rewards. The interaction-dense dataset collected through this tactile-driven curiosity yields strong zero-shot performance on downstream optimization tasks. We further use tactile-driven exploration to post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models. Although the VLAs are initially pre-trained without tactile feedback, post-training with \alg substantially improves downstream performance while remaining highly sample-efficient.
PaperID: 107,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.19641    
Authors:  Luke Rowe, Roger Girgis, Rodrigue de Schaetzen, Daphne Cornelisse, Alaap Grandhi, Felix Heide, Eugene Vinitsky, Christopher Pal, Liam Paull
Title: Scaling Self-Play for End-to-End Driving
Keywords: Autonomous driving and flight, Self-Play, Simulation
Abstract:
End-to-end autonomous driving models are typically trained on offline human-demonstration datasets that provide limited state coverage and often no closed-loop feedback, making them prone to compounding errors when deployed in closed-loop and brittle to long-tail agent interactions. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative strategy for training end-to-end driving models: large-scale self-play directly from pixels in simulation. While prior self-play approaches have shown promising transfer to real-world driving, they typically assume vectorized Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) observations that are incompatible with end-to-end policies operating directly on sensor observations. To this end, we introduce \emphGigapixel, a high-throughput batched driving simulator with perspective rendering, enabling scalable self-play directly from pixel observations. Rather than targeting compute-costly photorealistic sensor simulation, Gigapixel renders a simplified bounding-box world that preserves essential scene structure while achieving throughput at 50k agent steps per second. Since direct pixel-space self-play RL is prohibitively sample-inefficient at end-to-end model scale, we propose \emphself-play DAgger training: we train pixel-based policies in self-play via on-policy distillation from a privileged RL teacher. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we subsequently transfer the self-play trained policies to real-world sensor data through lightweight perception adaptation. Policies trained in Gigapixel and adapted to real-world sensor data achieve competitive performance on the HUGSIM and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks without human trajectory supervision. Moreover, scaling self-play training yields proportional gains in policy performance, establishing self-play as a practical and scalable strategy for training end-to-end models.
PaperID: 108,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Manav Gagvani, Benjamin Namikas, Sivamurugan Velmurugan, Nysa Kumar, Shrey Sharma, Thomas Peterson, Pratyush Mathur, Hyunseo Chang, Rohan Paleja
Title: Mechanistic Interpretability for End-to-End Self-Driving
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Autonomous driving and flight
Abstract:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models achieve strong planning performance but remain largely opaque, limiting observability and trust. We apply mechanistic interpretability to E2E driving by training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple, single-camera end-to-end path planning model. Unsupervised clustering of SAE latents reveals interpretable structure aligned with route intent, vehicle speed, and braking behavior, recovering driving intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision. Through paired counterfactual image edits, we further show that specific SAE features are visually grounded and systematically respond to scene changes such as traffic light state and stop sign presence. Steering individual SAE latents produces predictable, monotonic changes in planner outputs including lateral displacement, curvature, and braking. Finally, we demonstrate a practical application of these representations: we build a lightweight adapter trained on SAE latents that reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%, outperforming an equivalent adapter that omits SAE latents, confirming that the sparse representation captures useful information for interpretability.
PaperID: 109,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.20333    
Authors:  Jelena Trisovic, Rahel Rickenbach, Marek Landert, Panagiotis Minos, Melanie N. Zeilinger
Title: VIGOR-MPC: Vision-Guided Objective Regulation MPC
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Model Predictive Control, Vision-Based Control
Abstract:
Controlling an agent in an environment solely perceived through onboard vision is challenging: perception yields noisy, variable-length, and partially occluded context, while onboard compute is shared between perception and control, limiting the planning horizon executable in real time. We propose VIGOR-MPC, a modular student–teacher framework, agnostic to the perception pipeline, which distills a privileged, field-of-view-aware long-horizon MPC into a computationally lightweight short-horizon MPC whose cost parameters are determined online from vision. The teacher operates in simulation with full state knowledge and a multi-trajectory formulation that guarantees the agent can stay within its field of view. The student observes only the noisy, occluded context produced by a perception module and learns, via a recurrent mapping, to infer cost parameters that aim to recover the teacher's behavior despite missing information. We evaluate VIGOR-MPC on vision-based autonomous racing in simulation and on hardware. Using only onboard perception of the track, VIGOR-MPC generalizes to tracks unseen during training and approaches the lap times of the privileged long-horizon teacher while reducing per-step computation by over 90%.
PaperID: 110,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.07107    
Authors:  Jinhao wu, Shiduo Zhang, Yicheng Liu, Xiaopeng Yu, Sixian Li, Siyin Wang, Hang Zhao, Jingjing Gong, Xipeng Qiu
Title: Coarse-to-Control: Action-Token Planning for Vision-Language-Action Models
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Vision-Language-Action Model, Action Tokenization, Planning
Abstract:
Most vision-language-action (VLA) models map observations directly to actions without explicit intermediate planning, which limits performance on long-horizon tasks where early mistakes compound. We propose Coarse-to-Control, a plan-execute VLA that introduces planning natively in the action-token space. The key idea is to let the policy first predict a compact sequence of coarse action tokens that summarize the intended future trajectory, and then generate executable action tokens conditioned on this plan. Because both planning and execution share a unified discrete action vocabulary, the plan stays close to the control manifold and provides directly actionable guidance rather than an abstract hint that must be translated back to motor commands. Experiments on LIBERO, SimplerEnv-WidowX, and real-world manipulation tasks show that action-token planning consistently improves over direct action generation, with the largest gains on long-horizon multi-stage tasks.
PaperID: 111,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Yuxuan Xu, Jianzhe Gao, Hanlin Kong, Zhen Yin, Yonggen Ling, Wenguan Wang
Title: Compositional Diffusion Policy for Vision–Language–Action Agents
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Vision–Language–Action agents, Compositional Generalization
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) agents face a combinatorial task space where semantic and physical requirements are recombined in novel ways. However, existing holistic policies typically entangle them in a single latent representation, limiting generalization to unseen compositions and compromising physical feasibility. To this end, this work proposes an energy-based compositional diffusion policy that models robot action trajectory generation with distinct semantic and physical energy terms. Specifically, the agent factorizes multimodal inputs into grounded semantic factors and models them as implicit semantic energies. In parallel, it formulates physical constraints, including motion smoothness and kinematic manipulability, as explicit differentiable energies. These energies are jointly combined to guide trajectory generation toward both task satisfaction and physical feasibility. Our agent shows consistent improvements in compositional generalization and physical validity in real-world experiments and across some public benchmarks. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component. The code will be released. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of each component. The code will be released.
PaperID: 112,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.21924    
Authors:  Isabella Liu, An-Chieh Cheng, Rui Yan, Geng Chen, Ri-Zhao Qiu, Xueyan Zou, Sha Yi, Hongxu Yin, Xiaolong Wang, Sifei Liu
Title: Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Long-horizon manipulation remains challenging for vision-language-action (VLA) policies: real tasks are multi-step, progress-dependent, and brittle to compounding execution errors. We present LoHo-Manip, a modular framework that scales short-horizon VLA execution to long-horizon instruction following via a dedicated task-management VLM. The manager is decoupled from the executor and is invoked in a receding-horizon manner: given the current observation, it predicts a progress-aware remaining plan that combines (i) a subtask sequence with an explicit done + remaining split as lightweight language memory, and (ii) a visual trace—a compact 2D keypoint trajectory prompt specifying where to go and what to approach next. The executor VLA is adapted to condition on the rendered trace, thereby turning long-horizon decision-making into repeated local control by “following the trace.” Crucially, predicting the remaining plan at each step yields an implicit closed loop: failed steps persist in subsequent outputs, and traces update accordingly, enabling automatic continuation and replanning without hand-crafted recovery logic or brittle visual-history buffers. Extensive experiments spanning embodied planning, long-horizon reasoning, trajectory prediction, and end-to-end manipulation in simulation and on a real Franka robot demonstrate strong gains in long-horizon success, robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization.
PaperID: 113,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.15976    
Authors:  Anuva Banwasi, William Muckelroy III, Priya Sundaresan, Linfeng Zhao, Jeannette Bohg, Cherie Ho
Title: MessyMem: Learning-from-Doing Memory for Mobile Manipulation
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Mobile manipulation, Interaction-grounded memory
Abstract:
Mobile manipulators deployed at home across many rooms and many visits should improve with experience: after failing to open a locked cabinet, or finding an object in a drawer, the robot should use that knowledge to avoid repeated mistakes and complete future tasks more efficiently. However, today's robots often treat each task as new. Currently, compact scene representations omit interaction-derived knowledge, raw video buffers quickly grow to become inefficient and difficult to query, and VLM planners reason at inference time without persistently updating what the robot knows. Memory for mobile manipulation must be spatially grounded and queryable, updatable from interaction, and fine-grained enough to surface visual context that a text summary would lose. We present MessyMem, a memory system that enables mobile manipulators to learn from doing by building a compact 3D scene graph and associating it with learned interaction-derived properties and keyframes for visual detail. A task planner can use this memory to avoid repeated failures, reuse object locations, and recover visual context for long-horizon decisions. We evaluate MessyMem across multiple tasks in simulation and on a real mobile manipulator, showing that persistent interaction-grounded memory significantly improves long-horizon task success over representative baselines.
PaperID: 114,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.26545     GitHub
Authors:  Max Du, Zhanyi Sun, Chen Xu, Paarth Shah, Masha Itkina, Shuran Song
Title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), robotic continual learning, catastrophic forgetting
Abstract:
Robot policies deployed in-the-wild should have the capability to continually learn new tasks without forgetting existing behaviors. A common method to combat such catastrophic forgetting is to train on new task data with a replay buffer of previously learned task data. Although it is common to pick this buffer randomly from all prior experiences, our work shows that a small set of these experiences contributes greatly in anchoring past performance. We call these experiences, Memory Anchors. We propose identifying Memory Anchors as areas of representation collapse between the set of old and new task data that conflict in their required actions, like manipulating a familiar object in a new manner. The old data present in this region regularizes the new task training and prevents destructive overwriting of past task knowledge, serving as this critical Memory Anchor role. Removing access to 10% of these Memory Anchors in the replay buffer leads to more than a 4.5x increase in catastrophic forgetting on the LIBERO benchmark suites. We further demonstrate that enriching the replay buffer with Memory Anchors can decrease worst-case forgetting in LIBERO by 63% and lead to successful continual learning of highly-conflicting tasks on a real robot.
PaperID: 115,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.32027     GitHub
Authors:  Marcel Torne, Anubha Mahajan, Abhijnya Bhat, Chelsea Finn
Title: Freeform Preference Learning for Robotic Manipulation
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot manipulation, Preference Learning
Abstract:
Reward design remains a central bottleneck for autonomous robot policy improvement, especially in long-horizon manipulation tasks where sparse success labels provide too little signal and single binary preferences collapse many competing notions of quality into one ambiguous signal. We introduce Freeform Preference Learning (FPL), a method for learning robot policies from freeform human preferences. Rather than asking annotators which of two trajectories is better overall, FPL lets them define natural-language preference axes, such as speed, safety, formality, or carefulness, and provide pairwise preferences along each axis. These annotations are used to learn a language-conditioned reward model that maps a trajectory and preference label to an axis-specific reward. We use this model to train a reward-conditioned policy that can optimize across the multiple human-specified dimensions. Across four real-world and two simulated long-horizon manipulation tasks, FPL improves over sparse-reward and single-preference baselines by 38%. Beyond improved performance, FPL learns dense progress signals without explicit subtask segmentation, shows compositionality of behavior not present in the data, and allows users to steer the policy towards different behaviors at test time without retraining.
PaperID: 116,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21211     GitHub
Authors:  Dohyun Lee, Minho Park, Jeonghoon Park, Dongyoon Hwang, Junha Hyung, Sungwon Hwang, Byungkun Lee, Jaegul Choo
Title: Procedural Memory for Proactive Robot Assistance
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction
Abstract:
Proactive robot assistance requires acting on user needs before explicit requests, but zero-shot vision-language models struggle in this setting: lacking knowledge of the user's personal routine, they treat every situation as general and uncertain, defaulting to inaction rather than risking an incorrect intervention. We observe that everyday routines are highly repetitive, so even a few interactions reveal stable user-specific patterns that can ground proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a System 1--2 framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a \emphProcedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when and how to assist, and a VLA executor realizes the predicted task as low-level robot action. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. We evaluate on a multi-day desk-assistance scenario with six pick-and-place tasks. Memory-free baselines remain conservative across all five evaluation days, yielding near-zero recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Ablations further show that the FSM structure, rather than memory alone, is the primary driver of these gains.
PaperID: 117,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.24155    
Authors:  Jijie Li, Xu Yang, Junhong Zou, Chunhai Zhao, Chaoyang Zhao, Zhen Lei, Xiangyu Zhu
Title: Object-Centric Conditioning for Visuomotor Flow Matching
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Robot visuomotor policies are commonly formulated as autoregressive, diffusion-based, or more recently, flow matching models. Among them, Action-to-Action (A2A) flow matching improves inference efficiency by initializing generation from historical action priors rather than stochastic noise. However, strong dependence on historical motion priors, together with entangled global visual representations, can reduce robustness under spatial out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts and visual distractors. In this work, we propose SlotFlow, an object-centric flow matching policy for robust visuomotor manipulation. SlotFlow decouples scene observations into semantic (“what”) and geometric (“where“) representations to provide object-aware policy conditioning and object-centric spatial grounding. The semantic representation suppresses irrelevant background correlations, while the geometric representation improves adaptation to shifted object configurations under spatial perturbations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SlotFlow significantly improves robustness under visual distractors and severe spatial perturbations while preserving the low-step inference efficiency advantages of A2A flow matching in both simulation and real-world robotic manipulation tasks.
PaperID: 118,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Agastya Kalra, Ricardo Garcia-Pinel, Kirill Zaitsev, Pravin Dangol, Gjermund Ustensvik, Stephen Chow, Martin Bokeloh, Davin Tjandra, Huaijin Chen
Title: Z3P: Zero-Shot 3D-Object Perception for Robotics
Keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Learning representations for robotic perception and control
Abstract:
Tremendous progress has been made toward zero-shot, 3D-object-prompted perception tasks, including detection, segmentation, and 6D pose estimation. However, prior methods still struggle to see widespread use in robotics due to complexities such as challenging materials, dense clutter, and runtime. To address these limitations, we introduce Z3P, the first competitive end-to-end transformer architecture that performs zero-shot detection, segmentation, and pose estimation from single/multi-view RGB or RGB-D data and a 3D-object prompt. While previous methods use bounding boxes as an intermediate step between multiple models, Z3P operates as a single network that maintains an internal representation through persistent object tokens, allowing for better runtime and improved performance in densely cluttered environments with challenging materials. Across five robotic benchmarks (IPD, XYZ-IBD, ITODD-MV, T-ROBI, and ROBI), Z3P establishes a new state-of-the-art by becoming the first zero-shot method to outperform all prior zero-shot and object-specific approaches on detection and pose estimation. Finally, we demonstrate Z3P's utility as a foundation model for 3D-object perception, generalizing to multiple demanding robotic applications, including transparent object bin picking, sorting, car charging, and electronics assembly.
PaperID: 119,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05501     GitHub
Authors:  Emre Girgin, Cagri Kilic
Title: Learning Contact Representation for Leg Odometry
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Probabilistic learning and uncertainty in robotics, Leg Odometry, Contact Estimation
Abstract:
Leg odometry relies on the assumption that the velocity of a foot in stance is zero with respect to the world, which makes accurate contact detection a critical subproblem. Many approaches classify contact using ground reaction force (GRF) sensors at the foot tip, yet these sensors are not available on all legged robots and remain unresponsive to disturbances such as slippage while the foot is still in contact. Approaches without GRF sensing instead rely on heuristic pseudo-labels, model-based foot-velocity assumptions, or supervised contact learning. In this study, we propose a self-supervised representation learning framework for contact detection that uses only standard proprioceptive sensing (joint encoders and IMU) and requires neither force sensors nor contact labels. A denoising autoencoder is trained on kinematic features, a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model is fitted in the learned latent space, and its posterior is used as a continuous stance belief that scales the zero-velocity measurement covariance of an error-state Kalman filter. Experiments in simulation and on real-world terrain show that our framework yields the lowest odometry error among supervised and probabilistic baselines, and that higher pseudo-label classification accuracy does not translate into better downstream odometry. Our code and dataset are publicly available.
PaperID: 120,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.10755    
Authors:  Abhishek Joshi, Beining Han, Jack Nugent, Max Gonzalez Saez-Diez, Yiming Zuo, Jonathan Liu, Hongyu Wen, Stamatis Alexandropoulos, Karhan Kayan, Anna Calveri, Tao Sun, Gaowen Liu, Yi Shao, Alexander Raistrick, Jia Deng
Title: Procedural Generation of Articulated Simulation-Ready Assets
Keywords: Sim-to-real transfer, Robot manipulation, Articulated assets, Procedural generation
Abstract:
We introduce Infinigen-Articulated, a toolkit for generating realistic, procedurally generated articulated assets for robotics simulation. We include procedural generators for 18 common articulated object categories along with high-level utilities for use creating custom articulated assets in Blender. We also provide an export pipeline to integrate the resulting assets along with their physical properties into common robotics simulators. Experiments demonstrate that assets sampled from these generators are effective for movable object segmentation, training generalizable reinforcement learning policies, and sim-to-real transfer of imitation learning policies.
PaperID: 121,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.22630    
Authors:  Kyeongwon Park, Steven H. Collins
Title: Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
Keywords: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Physical human-robot interaction, Preference learning
Abstract:
Subjective user experience is important to human-robot interaction, but the outcomes users value, and how those preferences vary across individuals and contexts, are often unknown. While inverse learning approaches using human data can help identify user rewards, in many assistive settings the experimental costs of executing a control policy, measuring biomechanical or physiological outcomes, and collecting user feedback often limit the number of queries and optimization iterations. Here, we present Simultaneous Forward and Inverse Human-In-the-Loop Optimization (SFIHILO), which efficiently infers individual-specific reward functions from preferences over human outcomes and identifies a final control policy that maximizes the learned reward. SFIHILO bootstraps a forward model to predict user outcomes from control policies, uses this model for active querying to accelerate inverse reward learning, and then optimizes the final control policy without additional user trials. We score candidate policies by their expected reduction in uncertainty across both forward and inverse beliefs, targeting a regional preference boundary to robustly inform this simultaneous learning process. In simulation, we show that SFIHILO was effective across user heterogeneity, outcome dimensionalities, precision requirements, noise levels, and nonstationarity; compared with mutual information approaches, the proposed active querying strategy significantly improved sample efficiency in inverse learning while preserving forward model accuracy. This approach demonstrates the potential to infer latent human goals, enabling more transferable and effective human-robot interaction.
PaperID: 122,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.21740    
Authors:  Haru Kondoh, Kei Ota, Asako Kanezaki, Yueh-Hua Wu
Title: CounterAlign: Counterfactual Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Robot manipulation, Offline Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with behavior cloning (BC) on expert demonstrations. However, BC provides only positive supervision for expert actions, without explicit negative supervision indicating which actions are instruction-inconsistent or otherwise inappropriate. Reinforcement learning (RL) can provide such corrective signals, but often relies on externally specified rewards or curated non-expert data, both of which are costly to obtain in robotics. We show that offline RL for VLA models need not rely on curated non-expert trajectories: successful expert demonstrations alone can be transformed into dense corrective supervision through instruction relabeling. Specifically, by pairing expert actions with mismatched alternative instructions, we synthesize counterfactual instruction–observation–action tuples from the dataset and combine them with adversarial discriminator training to learn an instruction-grounded reward model for offline RL, without collecting additional rollouts or annotations. On the robustness-focused LIBERO-PRO benchmark, our method improves robustness to object position and task perturbations over a strong state-of-the-art baseline. It also outperforms competitive baselines in real-robot experiments on the TX-G2 (compatible with AGIBot G2). More broadly, our results suggest that, for data-constrained VLA learning, extracting denser supervision from each demonstration can complement collecting additional data.
PaperID: 123,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.24705    
Authors:  Chaoran Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Chenglin Cui, Yazhe Wan, Taein Kwon, Changjae Oh
Title: Relational Spatial Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control
Abstract:
Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the paradigm from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model's original expressivity. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and strong open-world generalization across diverse manipulation tasks.
PaperID: 124,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.13335    
Authors:  Libang Zhao, Qixin Zeng, Hongyin Zhang, Donglin Wang
Title: Information-Theoretic Constraints for Continual Vision-Language-Action Alignment
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Learning representations for robotic perception and control, continual learning, Vision language action
Abstract:
When deployed in open-ended robotic environments, Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models need to continually acquire new skills, yet suffer from severe catastrophic forgetting. We observe that this degradation is related to the deterioration of cross-modal information structure, where dependencies among visual observations, language instructions, and actions progressively diffuse during continual adaptation. But existing continual learning methods fail to preserve such cross-modal information dependencies. Thus, we propose Info-VLA, an information-preserving continual learning framework that maintains cross-modal information structure through dual constraints. Replay Anchor Contrastive Learning constructs stable alignment anchors from a frozen teacher model, preserving cross-modal alignment in the representation space. Cross-Modal Mutual Information Maximization further preserves dependency structure between visual and language representations through mutual information constraints. By jointly preserving historical alignment and cross-modal dependency information, Info-VLA balances stability and plasticity during continual learning. Furthermore, experiments on the simulators and real-world show that Info-VLA significantly outperforms existing methods in both task retention and adaptation.
PaperID: 125,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.12200    
Authors:  Andrew Kang, Priya Narasimhan
Title: Implicit Neural Representations of Individual Behavior
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Learning representations for robotic perception and control, policy representation, implicit neural representations
Abstract:
We study policy representation learning from unlabeled multi-policy behavioral data, where each episode is generated by a fixed but unobserved policy. We introduce Behavioral INR, a self-supervised generative model that adapts implicit neural representations from vision to behavior: instead of mapping coordinates to RGB values, it represents a policy as a state-action function mapping states to actions. An episode-level latent modulates this function through FiLM layers, yielding a generative prior over policies and enabling policy identity inference without labels. We also define policy-level out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts along state- and action-distribution axes, which arise when policies overlap but are not captured by standard agent- or environment-level OOD settings. Across synthetic GRF data, Seek-Avoid, MuJoCo, chess, Formula 1, and robotic manipulation, Behavioral INR most consistently improves policy identifiability in harder continuous state-action settings, especially when longer episodes, more policies, and OOD splits reduce marginal shortcuts. We will release code and checkpoints upon acceptance.
PaperID: 126,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.12978    
Authors:  Gokul Puthumanaillam, Vardhan Dongre, Pranay Thangeda, Hooshang Nayyeri, Dilek Hakkani-Tür, Melkior Ornik
Title: Trajectory-Level Redirection Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
Keywords: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Natural language instruction, Adversarial attacks
Abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models bring natural language into closed-loop robot control, enabling robots to execute manipulation tasks directly from text instructions. The same interface gives text a recurring role in control because the prompt is reused at every replanning step, and each prompt-conditioned action changes the future observations on which the policy acts. Existing VLA attacks study adversarial prompts that elicit targeted low-level actions or make such actions persist across changing images. We identify a stronger trajectory-level failure mode: a prompt that still appears to specify the intended task but redirect the final physical outcome. We mathematically formalize this setting as command-preserving trajectory redirection, a prompt-only threat model in which the attacker chooses one prompt before the episode, all policy and environment components remain fixed, and the prompt must stay close to the benign instruction while omitting target words and correction language. To find such prompts, we introduce an on-policy prompt search method that uses rollouts to discover perturbations whose closed-loop behavior tracks a target task while satisfying the command-preserving constraints. Experiments in simulation and on hardware show that near-benign prompt perturbations can redirect VLA rollouts to attacker-specified targets. These results expose a trajectory-level vulnerability in VLA instruction grounding: text that appears to preserve the intended command can still give an adversary control over the robot's final physical outcome.
PaperID: 127,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23888     GitHub GitHub
Authors:  Jing Xiong, Jiale Xie, Haoqi Yuan, Chaoyi Xu, Zongqing Lu
Title: MoDex: Towards Universal Multi-Object Dexterous Grasping
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Multi-object grasping
Abstract:
Multi-object grasping is a fundamental yet challenging problem, constrained by data collection costs, varying spatial layouts, and the need for broad generalization. To address these challenges, we propose MoDex, a data-efficient framework that provides the first unified solution for universal multi-object dexterous grasping across diverse spatial layouts. MoDex accomplishes this by formulating the task as a single-step decision problem of learning residual corrections to a reference trajectory, and introducing a spatially adaptive dual-strategy that performs single-shot grasping for proximal objects and sequential interaction for separated objects. Extensive evaluations show that MoDex significantly outperforms baselines in proximal configurations, achieving 64.17% success on unseen objects, and uniquely succeeds in separated layouts where prior methods struggle. Further experiments demonstrate its generalization across robot embodiments, scalability and zero-shot sim-to-real deployment through a vision-based policy trained solely on simulation data.
PaperID: 128,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Vongani Hlavutelo Maluleke, James Ni, Kie Horiuchi, Lea Wilken, Jiahui Lei, Evonne Ng, Roei Herzig, Jitendra Malik, Trevor Darrell, Angjoo Kanazawa
Title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human–Humanoid Interaction
Keywords: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction
Abstract:
Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Our approach decomposes the problem into a high-level policy and a low-level policy. For the high-level policy, we introduce a shared-codebook VQ-VAE that tokenizes human and humanoid motion into a unified latent space, enabling cross-embodiment conditional generation via a Diffusion Forcing Transformer. The low-level policy uses a whole-body tracking controller for deployment on the Unitree G1. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of paired human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world.
PaperID: 129,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.00374     GitHub
Authors:  Daniel Morton, Pranit Mohnot, Marco Pavone
Title: Constrained Whole-Body Tracking for Humanoid Robots
Keywords: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems, Reinforcement learning for physical robot control
Abstract:
Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) have demonstrated impressive whole-body agility for humanoid robots, yet ensuring safety and satisfying constraints -- particularly those specified after training -- remains a challenge. Towards this goal, we present ConstrainedMimic, a control framework that leverages whole-body kinematics and dynamics for real-time constraint enforcement within RL tracking policies. By integrating principles from operational space control and control barrier functions (CBFs), we enable the satisfaction of arbitrary runtime constraints on both the kinematic reference motion and the underlying dynamics. In whole-body motion-tracking and teleoperation experiments on a (simulated) Unitree G1 with a learned policy, we demonstrate collision avoidance (both with the robot body and external obstacles), joint limits, and center of mass stability constraints. By remaining consistent with the current contact mode and tracking objectives, we minimally restrict the capabilities of the policy when constraints are active. Our method is fully differentiable, runs on CPU, GPU, and TPU, and can be deployed at up to 300-500 Hz. All software will be freely available upon publication.
PaperID: 130,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Gio Huh, Yue Zhuo, Zehua Wang, Alan Yu, Yibo Cheng, Yanbing Han, Gabriel B. Margolis, Ge Yang
Title: Learning Functional Compliance in Whole-body Manipulation
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control
Abstract:
Compliant whole-body controllers for humanoids achieve safety by uniformly relaxing stiffness across all directions, but this dissolves the control authority needed for contact-rich tasks, forcing a hard trade-off between safety and performance. We introduce functional compliance: a task-dependent compliant control scheme that preserves authority along task-relevant axes while staying compliant elsewhere, varying in both direction and time. We simultaneously learn a control policy using a reward shaped by compliant poses and a force estimator that can be used at deploy time to compose variable compliance profiles. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three contact-rich whole-body manipulation tasks on the Unitree G1. Our method matches state-of-the-art motion-tracking fidelity while improving task success on key insertion and book reorientation, where directional and time-varying compliance is required, and matching the strongest baseline on cabinet opening, where it is not. This suggests that task-specific variable compliance, not constant uniform relaxation, is the correct whole-body control primitive for humanoid manipulation.
PaperID: 131,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Lixing Fang, Ziyan Xiong, Sunli Chen, Zhiyang Dou, Chuang Gan
Title: SPOT: Spatial Perception-Oriented Long-Horizon Humanoid Teleoperation
Keywords: Robotic data generation
Abstract:
High-quality demonstration data is becoming a central bottleneck for training general-purpose humanoid robots. While recent humanoid teleoperation systems have made substantial progress in retargeting human motion to robot motion, long-horizon loco-manipulation requires another capability: operators must maintain task-relevant spatial awareness over time, e.g., object locations, surrounding environments, the robot's pose. We call the extent of this awareness the operator's perceptual horizon. However, existing methods often shorten this: narrow views miss peripheral events, robot-mounted cameras become unstable during locomotion, and coupled head-view control makes looking around interfere with robot motion. We present SPOT, a Spatial Perception-Oriented VR Teleoperation system for collecting long-horizon humanoid demonstration data by providing extended perceptual horizon. SPOT combines a robot-mounted binocular fisheye camera, a wide-field stereoscopic display, viewpoint-decoupled free-looking, and visual stabilization to provide a robot-centric view that is wide, stable, and actively inspectable. Unlike conventional egocentric interfaces, SPOT decouples visual exploration from robot actuation: the egocentric stereo observation is rendered on a virtual hemisphere around the operator, so natural head rotations change where the operator looks within the wide-field view rather than commanding the robot head, camera, or torso. We evaluate SPOT on perception-critical humanoid data-collection tasks spanning drop recovery, peripheral retrieval, large-workspace bimanual manipulation, fine alignment, and dynamic interaction. SPOT improves efficiency, accuracy, recovery speed, and operator workload, demonstrating its effectiveness for user-friendly and scalable long-horizon humanoid data collection.
PaperID: 132,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Shashank A Deshpande, JONATHAN P HOW
Title: Self-Supervised Dispersive Sampling for Kinodynamic Search
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Autonomous driving and flight
Abstract:
Control-space tree search sidesteps the steering requirement of geometric search methods and offers an asymptotic route to natively feasible kinodynamic trajectories. In practice, however, control-space search fails on the simplest of motion-planning instances for nonlinear systems such as quadrotors. This failure is rooted in poor geometric coverage induced when naive control-sampling measures are pushed forward through system dynamics. We resolve this problem by learning a lightweight sampler whose pushforward achieves low geometric dispersion in the local search space. The central idea is to utilize a well-dispersed reference map as a training scaffold, eliminating the need for an external expert. Our experiments then demonstrate that the learned sampler enables control-space search for quadrotor motion planning when naive sampling measures simply fail. Once enabled, control-space planning is shown to generate highly agile trajectory solutions in an obstacle-dense setting as compared to established trajectory optimization techniques. We also show that the geometric reach of the learned model dominates popular motion primitive libraries, spanning roughly thrice their volume. Arbitrarily low-dispersion primitives are thus made available for any state merely by scaling test-time compute.
PaperID: 133,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.03208    
Authors:  Wancong Zhang, Basile Terver, Artem Zholus, Soham Chitnis, Harsh Sutaria, Mido Assran, Randall Balestriero, Amir Bar, Yann LeCun, Nicolas Ballas
Title: Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models
Keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Combination of learning and planning in robotics
Abstract:
World models are a promising path to zero-shot embodied control through planning. However, existing world model planners struggle on long-horizon, multi-stage tasks: prediction errors compound and naive search is exponential in the planning horizon. Hierarchy mitigates both by decomposing tasks into shorter, tractable subproblems; yet prior hierarchical approaches either amortize control into task-specific policies (hierarchical RL) or assume low-dimensional states and known dynamics (classical hierarchical MPC). We present Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models (HWM), an architecture and planning paradigm for hierarchical model predictive control (MPC) directly on visual world models trained solely via next-latent prediction. HWM learns world models at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, so predictions from the long horizon model serve as subgoals for the short horizon model via latent matching—without task-specific rewards, skill learning, or hierarchical policies. To keep long-horizon search tractable, HWM learns an action encoder that compresses primitive action chunks into latent macro-actions. On real-world Franka manipulation, HWM solves pick-&-place from a single goal image at 70% success vs. 0% for single-level planning. Across simulated push manipulation and maze navigation, HWM consistently improves performance on long-horizon tasks while requiring up to 3× less planning compute.
PaperID: 134,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.22535     GitHub
Authors:  Byungjun Kim, Taeksoo Kim, Hyunsoo Cha, Hanbyul Joo
Title: Robot-Factored World Models via Robot Rendering
Keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Robotic data generation, Robotic action-contitioned world models
Abstract:
Action-conditioned video world models predict future observations from an initial observation and an action signal. In robotics, this action signal becomes future video in two stages: a robot body and controller realize it as motion, and the scene responds through contact, occlusion, and object motion. Conditioning directly on the pre-realization signal asks the video model to learn robot-specific controller semantics, while conditioning on logged future states leaks interaction outcomes. We propose robot-factored world models, which target the middle signal: a deployment-available nominal trajectory produced by the robot's own controller and kinematics before observing scene interaction. Together with camera-aware static RGB/depth context, this rendered nominal geometry forms a shared visual world-model interface for fixed and dynamic viewpoints. The video model sees the action only as visible nominal geometry, and learns how objects, surfaces, and occlusions change around it. On DROID and RoboCasa-GR1, this rendered interface improves over Cartesian/vector action-conditioning baselines, while motion-source and depth ablations isolate the value of nominalization and 3D contact cues. We further probe the same rendered-prompt interface through counterfactual trajectory redirection, held-out embodiment composition, and human demonstration to robot video.
PaperID: 135,   Poster  OpenReview   GitHub
Authors:  jielin wu, Shenzhe Yao, Guanqi He, Xiaohan Liu, Zhaoqing Zeng, Xiangrui Jiang, Han Yang, Wentao Zhang, Hang Zhao
Title: TopoRetarget: Interaction-centric retarget for dexterous manipulation
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Motion Retargeting
Abstract:
Human hand-object demonstrations provide dense reference motions for training dexterous manipulation RL policies through reference tracking. However, to use such demonstrations for robot policy learning, retargeting must preserve more than hand pose and maintain the object-relative interaction structure that defines task execution. Otherwise, contact and feasibility artifacts can propagate into downstream RL training. We introduce TopoRetarget, an interaction-centric retargeting framework that uses a single parameter set across diverse retargeting conditions while preserving task-relevant local hand-object topology and adapting human demonstrations to dexterous robot hands. The method constructs a sparse interaction graph over hand and object keypoints and optimizes distance-weighted Laplacian deformation with directional consistency, kinematic constraints, and penetration handling. Evaluations show that the generated references improve both interaction fidelity and policy learning: TopoRetarget achieves the best contact precision and alignment over all baselines on the ContactPose Dataset, improves Pen-Spin training success by 40.6 percentage points over the existing baseline methods, and enables zero-shot transfer to Wuji Hand hardware on cube reorientation and pen spinning. Project website:https://toporetarget2026.github.io/TopoRetarget/
PaperID: 136,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Kai Ma, Hang Su, Chengyang Ying, Ruyi Gan, Hao Wang, Jun Zhu
Title: TUTOR: Learning Recovery from Policy-Induced Deviations
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot manipulation, Vision-language-action models, Human-in-the-loop robot learning
Abstract:
Supervised fine-tuning gives vision-language-action (VLA) policies strong manipulation skills in demonstration-like states, but deployment on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks often exposes compounding errors. Small action mistakes can move the robot off the demonstration manifold, where locally plausible action chunks may continue driving the system toward failure. We present TUTOR, a human-in-the-loop post-training method that uses intervention episodes to repair such policy-induced failures. Rather than treating an intervention only as a corrective demonstration, TUTOR also reuses the autonomous rollout before takeover as signed evidence about the policy's behavior. A hindsight keypoint partitions each rollout into recoverable chunks to preserve and failure-inducing chunks to reject, while the human takeover provides verified recovery chunks to imitate. TUTOR trains on these three signals with a negative-aware flow-matching objective. Failed rollout chunks are suppressed by a lagged-reference repulsion term tied to the policy snapshot that generated them, and recovery chunks are fit with standard flow-matching imitation. On a 14-DoF dual-arm tabletop platform with three long-horizon, contact-rich tasks, TUTOR improves autonomous success from 8.3% to 35.0% over supervised fine-tuning, under the same online-episode budget and takeover interface as the intervention baseline. Ablations show that rollout negatives and human recovery data provide complementary gains, while SFT preservation mainly stabilizes updates.
PaperID: 137,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.10137     GitHub GitHub
Authors:  Liuao Pei, Tianyue Wu, Hui Zhang, Ping Luo, Jie Song
Title: Assembling Two Parts in One Hand
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot manipulation, Dexterous manipulation, Sim-to-real reinforcement learning
Abstract:
A hallmark of human dexterity is the cooperative use of fingers, where different fingers take on distinct yet coordinated roles to accomplish fine manipulation, such as capping a pen with the hand that holds it. We study this finger-level coordination through \emphin-hand assembly: mating two rigid objects within a single dexterous hand, with no second arm and no fixture. We present a reinforcement learning formulation to solve this problem in a unified framework, which is driven by a goal relative pose between the two parts.
