Authors:  Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Schmidt, Hang Yu, Ye Jin, Sajad Marvi, Georg Martius, Julian Jordan
Title: DriveMLP: When Training Strategy Outperforms Model Complexity in Autonomous Driving
Keywords: Autonomous driving and flight, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Demonstration-based Reinforcement Learning, Ego-vehicle planning
Abstract:
Learning motion planning policies that remain reliable under closed-loop execution is a central challenge in Autonomous Driving (AD). Imitation Learning (IL) scales well to large AD datasets but suffers from distribution shift, causal confusion, and compounding errors under closed-loop execution. In contrast, Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically requires handcrafted rule-based rewards and massive simulation. We introduce a simple closed-loop IL framework that uses RL purely as an optimization tool, guided by a trajectory-distance reward derived from logged expert data. A lightweight MLP policy trained with our method achieves a score of 86.51 on the nuPlan Val14 Reactive benchmark, a +3.2 point improvement over the previous best IL planner (Flow Planner), with >15x faster inference. Our central finding is that training strategy plays a role at least as important as model complexity: closed-loop optimization with trajectory-based supervision is sufficient to outperform recent large-scale generative IL planners while dramatically reducing inference cost. Code and trained models will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
PaperID: 512,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.02222    
Authors:  Haokun Liu, Zhaoqi MA, Yicheng Chen, Wentao Zhang, masaki kitagawa, XIONGZICEN, Jinjie Li, MOJU ZHAO
Title: CoFL-S: Spatially Queryable Sector Flow Fields for Local Language-Conditioned Navigation
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Robot navigation and locomotion, Vision-Language Navigation, Flow Field Policy
Abstract:
Vision-Language Navigation has increasingly emphasized high-level instruction reasoning, memory, global map construction, and instruction decomposition, while the low-level action representation remains comparatively underexplored. We propose CoFL-S, a low-level vision-language-action framework that predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot's local visible sector and generates continuous trajectories by rolling out the predicted field. To train this low-level representation, we convert each VLN-CE episode, originally a whole-episode instruction paired with an action sequence, into frame-level local supervision with aligned sub-instructions and matched action, trajectory, and dense flow-field targets. For evaluation, we introduce a continuous-time Habitat benchmark that isolates low-level action interfaces from instruction decomposition and executes all methods through a shared velocity-command controller, enabling decomposition-independent closed-loop comparison across different planner frequencies rather than fixed discrete forward-and-turn transitions in VLN-CE. Under matched encoders and training settings, CoFL-S consistently outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark, and zero-shot real-world closed-loop deployment further shows its advantage over both baselines beyond simulation.
PaperID: 513,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Yuhang Wang, Lingyao Li, Hao Zhou
Title: Observe Before You Alert: Belief-State Driver Alerting with Vision–Language Models
Keywords: Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems, Autonomous driving and flight, Driving Alert System, Driving safety benchmark
Abstract:
Driver alerting from dashcam video is a sequential decision problem under partial observability: a system must warn early enough to support driver response, while avoiding frequent nuisance alerts. Existing approaches often reduce this problem to binary risk prediction, forcing a thresholded silent-or-alert decision even when visual evidence is incomplete. We propose VLAlert, a vision-language framework that formulates driver alerting as a tri-action policy over Silent, Observe, and Alert. The Observe action serves as an internal evidence-gathering state, allowing the system to defer uncertain warnings and adapt its subsequent observation window before issuing a driver-facing alert. VLAlert adapts a 4B vision-language model to generate structured safety-evidence spans and uses hidden states pooled from these spans as compact belief representations for danger estimation and policy prediction. To evaluate alerting beyond threshold-free anticipation metrics, we construct VLAlert-Bench, a unified per-tick benchmark from multiple driving-alert datasets, and introduce DAUS, a driver-aware utility score that jointly measures ranking, video coverage, false-alert burden, and lead-time utility. Experiments show that VLAlert achieves the best overall operating-point utility among representative video and VLM baselines. Ablations further indicate that structured belief-span pooling improves alert separability and that retaining Observe as a separate action provides useful supervision for uncertain pre-alert states.
PaperID: 514,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Yanan Hao, Wenjiang Xu, Pengfei Yi, Wanting Li, Yaxiong Wu
Title: DualSpace-VLA: Coupling Cartesian-Space Motion Intent with Joint-Space Execution in Vision-Language-Action Policies
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Robot manipulation, Vision-Language-Action Models, Action Space Design
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made rapid progress in grounding language-conditioned visual observations into robot action chunks. Yet the action interface directly shapes how these chunks are learned and executed on physical robots. Cartesian end-effector space provides an object-centric and geometrically meaningful representation of motion intent, but executing Cartesian actions on joint-controlled robots requires an additional inverse-kinematics layer, which can yield non-unique or less stable joint targets on redundant robots. Joint-space actions are directly compatible with low-level controllers, but can obscure task-level motion structure and require policies to internalize embodiment-specific kinematics. This creates a trade-off for single-space VLAs between clear motion intent and stable execution. To address this trade-off, we introduce DualSpace-VLA, a dual-space VLA framework that uses Cartesian-space motion intent to guide executable joint-space action generation. DualSpace-VLA predicts Cartesian motion-intent tokens from VLM representations under chunk-wise delta end-effector supervision and injects these tokens into a flow-matching joint-action expert through intent-guided cross-attention and gated fusion. Differentiable forward kinematics further maps generated joint trajectories to Cartesian end-effector trajectories, providing a trajectory-level geometric regularizer during training without inverse kinematics at inference time. Extensive experiments in RoboTwin simulation, real-world bimanual manipulation, and few-shot transfer to a low-cost embodiment show that DualSpace-VLA outperforms both end-effector-only and joint-only VLA baselines.
PaperID: 515,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.37165     GitHub
Authors:  Junghyun Kim, Ngseo Kim, Chungwoo Lee, Seoyeon Lee, Woo-Jeong Baek, Adam Zhou, Chip Huyen, Jun Ki Lee, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
Title: Disentangling Spurious Correlations in Vision-Language-Action Models via Predicting Domain-Invariant Latent Lookahead
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Vision-Language-Action Models, Shortcut Learning
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models remain brittle under visual distribution shifts, often relying on spurious correlations tied to domain-specific factors rather than task-relevant structure. We propose Domain-Invariant Latent Lookahead (DILL), a representation-learning framework that mitigates shortcut learning in VLA policies. Our key idea is to supervise policies with domain-invariant future latents learned from domain-transformed trajectory data. A Task-Domain Encoder is trained with contrastive objectives and Gaussian disentanglement regularization to separate task-relevant structure from domain-specific visual variation. The learned encoder then provides future latents for VLA policy learning through lookahead prediction and domain disentanglement, encouraging the policy to focus on task-relevant structure rather than incidental visual factors. Under counterfactual task--view compositions, DILL reduces shortcut degree while improving OOD success. On LIBERO-Plus visual perturbations, DILL achieves the highest average success rate of 69.1%, outperforming the strongest matched-input baseline by 11.4 absolute points, while limiting the average performance drop to 12.5 points. Latent-space diagnostics further show that DILL better preserves task-consistent structure while suppressing domain-specific variation.
PaperID: 516,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.10655    
Authors:  Xiatao Sun, Yuan Zhuang, Mateo Sanchez Lopez Negrete, Matei-Victor Coldea, Chen Liang, Haoyang Zhang, Che Liu, Ziyao Zeng, Shawn Li, Qian Wang, Fei Miao, Daniel Rakita
Title: Artificial Foveated Perception for Mitigating Shortcut Learning in Robotic Foundation Models
Keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Shortcut Learning, Generalizability
Abstract:
Robotic foundation models have recently made substantial progress in multi-task capability, cross-embodiment transfer, and language-conditioned control. Yet deploying these models robustly across diverse real-world settings remains difficult, in part because policies often fail to distinguish between causally relevant visual structure and spurious scene-level correlations. For instance, a policy trained to pick up a mug may fail when the table is shifted, the room becomes dimmer, or previously unseen distractors appear nearby. We identify this failure mode as shortcut learning: the tendency of a model to exploit predictive but non-causal correlations in the training distribution rather than the task-relevant visual evidence that determines successful action. Although shortcut learning has been extensively studied in computer vision and broader machine learning, its role in robotic foundation models remains comparatively underexplored. In this paper, we study shortcut learning as a central obstacle to scalable robotic foundation models and propose Artificial Foveated Perception (AFP) as a direct intervention in the perception pipeline. AFP is a lightweight, policy-agnostic module that takes the same vision and language inputs as existing Vision-Language-Action and World Action Model pipelines and predicts task-conditioned masks over relevant objects, the robot, and other action-critical regions. These masks can be used for visual preprocessing, token filtering, attention modulation, or auxiliary grounding losses, enabling AFP to suppress task-irrelevant visual evidence without modifying the core policy architecture. We evaluate AFP across state-of-the-art robotic foundation models and show that foveating perception reduces fine-tuning time, suppresses overfitting, and improves generalization under environmental perturbations. Through ablations over integration modes and mask usage, we further show that these gains arise from directing policy learning and inference toward task-relevant visual regions. These results suggest that task-conditioned foveated perception is a practical mechanism for making robotic foundation models more robust, data-efficient, and scalable.
PaperID: 517,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13422     GitHub
Authors:  Zheyu Zhuang, Ruiyu Wang, Nick Heppert, Johannes Fabian Hahn, Abhinav Valada, Florian T. Pokorny, Danica Kragic
Title: Attention from Action, for Action: Emergent Visual Bottlenecks for Policy Learning
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Robot manipulation, Region of Interest
Abstract:
Visual bottlenecks that focus policy inputs on regions of interest (ROIs) can improve data-efficient visuomotor learning by separating where to look from how to act. Many ROI interfaces rely on external spatial labels, such as gaze, object classes, or affordance annotations. Label-free alternatives often derive crops from trajectories by detecting gripper or motion events and centering a fixed crop at the projected end-effector. Such action-derived crops are useful spatial priors that require no additional labels, but they encode fixed choices about event timing, proxy points, and crop scale. When the visual evidence needed for control lies away from the end-effector or changes continuously with task progress, these crops can become misaligned. We propose Seeker, a task- and state-conditioned readout that learns attention from action. Starting from frozen DINO features, Seeker iteratively updates a query with gathered visual evidence, producing progression-aware ROIs solely from action supervision. The learned ROI serves as a spatial interface for RGB cropping, mask-guided background augmentation, and point-cloud filtering. Across simulation and real-robot experiments, Seeker improves data efficiency and robustness over no-crop, augmentation, and action-derived crop baselines. On real robots, Seeker raises average in-domain success from the best baseline's 48.3 to 76.7% and success under lighting/background shifts from 20.0 to 60.0%.
PaperID: 518,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Yi Yang, Zhihong Liu, Siqi Kou, Yiyang Chen, Yanzhe Hu, Jianbo Zhou, Boyuan Zhao, Zhijie Wei, XIA Xiao, Xueqi Li, Pengfei Liu, Zhijie Deng
Title: World-Language-Action Model for Unified World Modeling, Language Reasoning, and Action Synthesis
Keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)
Abstract:
We propose world-language-action (WLA) models as a new class of embodied foundation models. WLA takes textual instructions, images, and robot states as inputs to jointly predict textual subtasks, subgoal images, and robot actions, conjoining the \emphworld modeling interface to learn from extensive egocentric videos as in the world-action model (WAM) and the \emphlanguage reasoning capacities to solve complex long-horizon tasks as in vision-language-action (VLA) models. At the core of WLA lies an \emphauto-regressive (AR) Transformer backbone, instead of a bidirectional diffusion Transformer as in WAMs, to predict the \emphnext-state, comprising the \emphsemantic-level textual intention and complementary \emphfine-grained physical dynamics. The physical dynamics are supervised by the world modeling objective based on a dedicated World Expert, and are leveraged to ease the characterization of the state-action correlation for the Action Expert. WLA leverages meta-queries to make the world prediction \emphimplicitly impact the action generation so that the former can be disabled during inference. The world prediction can also be activated to enable test-time scaling for improved robot control. Our WLA-0 prototype, with 2B active parameters, achieves 40 ms per inference on an NVIDIA RTX 5090. Evaluations across simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that WLA-0 achieves state-of-the-art multi-task and long-horizon learning abilities, e.g., 92.94% success rate on RoboTwin2.0 Clean and 56.5% success rate on RMBench. WLA-0 also holds the promise to learn novel tasks directly from \emphcross-embodiment robot videos without action annotations.
PaperID: 519,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Haomin Zuo, Wenzhan Li, Ruimao Zhang, Yulan Guo
Title: PAWN: Preference-Aware Semantic NFT for Online Reinforcement Learning of Flow-based VLAs
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Online reinforcement learning for flow-based manipulation policies is challenging because multi-step solver-based action generation makes the action likelihoods required by standard policy-ratio objectives difficult to access. Hopefully, NFT-style methods offer a promising likelihood-free route for local policy optimization, and recent embodied extensions have begun to adapt this idea to flow-based robot policies. However, several structural issues remain: trajectory-level outcomes provide noisy and misaligned credit for action chunks and their intermediate solver states; full-space mirrored comparisons ignore the compositional geometry of robot actions; and local updates may still follow noisy behavior-sampled continuations without explicitly identifying better alternatives, which may be guided toward the manifold of suboptimal actions. We present Preference-Aware Semantic NFT (PAWN), a unified NFT-style online RL framework that addresses these issues through structured local preference optimization. PAWN derives implicit chunk-level preference signals by lifting solver-step density comparisons to chunk-path scores, reorganizes mirrored local evidence into SE(3)-aware motion modes, and uses conditional pair guidance to favor locally better continuations. Experiments on flow-based manipulation benchmarks show consistent gains in adaptation efficiency, final success, and OOD robustness over strong online RL baselines.
PaperID: 520,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Justin Fletcher
Title: Telescopes are Optomechanical Robots: Training Compositional Visuomotor Policies for Coordinated Control
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Robotics for scientific instruments, Optomechanical control
Abstract:
Direct imaging of Earth-like exoplanets requires 10 milliarcsecond angular resolution and 10^-9 contrast; engineering a single telescope that simultaneously exhibits the aperture baseline and wavefront control needed to meet both requirements has proven challenging. We build on recent advances in distributed-aperture interferometer designs to recast the problem as a high-dimensional visuomotor optomechanical robotic control task: many physically separate mirror segments must be aligned to within a small fraction of the observing wavelength, given only science path focal plane imagery. We train recurrent visuomotor policies with PPO to phase such a telescope end-to-end from the interferometric focal-plane image. Direct application of these methods to the full forty-five-DOF, fifteen-segment problem is ineffective; instead we train fifteen per-segment alignment skill policies, each articulating three actuators, and compose them at inference into a single 240-step rollout. The same policy architecture, with a target-conditioning input and a modified reward, is able to perform directed wavefront shaping to suppress flux in designated dark-hole regions by approximately two orders of magnitude across many target regions. A coarse-to-fine variant of the same pattern co-phases a two-segment aperture from 2 arcsec initial differential motion in a median of fifteen control steps, approximately five orders of magnitude faster than an online-optimization baseline.
PaperID: 521,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Ruicong Liu, Yifei Huang, Liangyang Ouyang, Caixin Kang, Yoichi Sato
Title: Predictive Representation Learning for Manipulation via Streaming Egocentric 3D Hand Forecasting
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Task and motion planning, Egocentric vision, hand pose forecasting
Abstract:
Learning embodied manipulation from egocentric human data offers a scalable path, reducing the cost of collecting robot-specific demonstrations. However, existing representation learning methods largely stop at perceptual understanding, such as extracting what a scene contains or what an action is. A capable embodied agent is more than understanding: it predicts the next motion. We propose that forecasting 3D human hand motion is one suitable pretraining task, as the representation jointly learns how to manipulate objects and how the motion will unfold next. Building on this hypothesis, we introduce SFHand, the first representation learning method via streaming egocentric 3D hand forecasting. SFHand learns by autoregressively predicting future 3D hand states, including hand type, 2D bounding box, 3D pose, and trajectory, from a continuous stream of video and language instructions. Its autoregressive architecture is equipped with an ROI-enhanced memory layer, capturing temporal context while focusing on salient hand-centric regions. To enable this research, we also introduce EgoHaFL the first open-source large-scale dataset pairing synchronized 3D hand poses with fine-grained language instructions (247K clips, 3.95M frames). Transferred to downstream embodied control, the learned representation shows state-of-the-art performance on both simulation and real-world manipulation benchmarks, improving success rate by up to 13.4%. Our method also achieves leading 3D hand forecasting accuracy, with 35.8% lower ADE than baseline methods. These results suggest that forecasting hand motion is a better pretraining task for representation learning in embodied manipulation. The code and data will be released.
PaperID: 522,   Poster  OpenReview   GitHub
Authors:  Dian Wang, Jisang Park, Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Shuran Song, Jeannette Bohg
Title: Mixture of Frames Policy: Multi-Frame Action Denoising for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Robotic manipulation is inherently multi-frame: local actions may be simple in an end-effector frame, while transport, upright-object handling, and whole-body coordination are better represented in a base-aligned frame. However, modern diffusion-based visuomotor policies typically commit to a single predefined action frame, forcing one denoiser to model action distributions that are often unnecessarily complex in that frame. We propose Mixture of Frames Policy (MoF), a diffusion policy that performs synchronized action denoising across multiple coordinate frames. MoF maintains a single canonical diffusion state, re-expresses it in several task-relevant frames, applies frame-specialized denoisers, and fuses their noise predictions back in the canonical frame. To make this possible for intermediate noisy diffusion states, we introduce a column-based 6D rotation representation within an SE(3) action parameterization that supports exact, differentiable frame transformations without requiring noisy rotations to lie on the SO(3) manifold. Across nine simulated bimanual manipulation tasks, we show that the best action frame is task-dependent and that MoF improves over oracle frame selection and standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) baselines. We further evaluate MoF on two real-world bimanual mobile manipulation tasks, demonstrating that it outperforms all constituent single-frame baselines. Project homepage: \hrefhttps://mof-policy.github.iomof-policy.github.io.
PaperID: 523,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.27890     GitHub
Authors:  Woo Chul Shin, Zhenyang Chen, Alfred Cueva, Nadun Ranawaka Arachchige, Yingyan Celine Lin, Benjamin Joffe, Shreyas Kousik, Danfei Xu
Title: Static In, Dynamic Out: Counterfactual Action Augmentation for Moving Object Manipulation
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Visuomotor policies have advanced on manipulation tasks where the target object stays static during execution, but real deployments break this assumption: parts drift on conveyors and fruits sway in the wind. We introduce Static In, Dynamic Out (SIDO), a counterfactual action augmentation that enables a policy trained only on static object demonstrations to adapt to unseen object motion at test time. Our key idea is to factorize moving object manipulation into two sub-problems: predicting where the object will be, and reaching that predicted pose. SIDO displaces the object to a counterfactual future position and morphs the demonstrated action chunk to preserve the hand-object relative pose, yielding a goal-conditioned policy. At deployment an object pose predictor supplies the future position. Across three simulated tasks (Mug, Square, Stack) under five object motion patterns and two real-world tasks (Gantry, Peachtree), SIDO improves moving object success over the baselines while preserving static object performance. Project website: https://sido-staticindynamicout.github.io/
PaperID: 524,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.12603    
Authors:  Honglin He, Zhizheng Liu, Yukai Ma, Bolei Zhou
Title: From Imitation to Alignment: Human-Preference Flow Policies for Long-Horizon Sidewalk Navigation
Keywords: Robot navigation and locomotion, Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems
Abstract:
Autonomous long-horizon sidewalk navigation is essential for micro-mobility applications such as robotic food delivery and assistive electronic wheelchairs. Unlike autonomous driving on the road, long-horizon sidewalk navigation requires precise maneuvering through unpredictable sidewalk terrains and pedestrians, with a lightweight perception stack as minimal as a single monocular RGB camera. While imitation learning (IL) from demonstrations offers a practical solution, the resulting autopilot policy often suffers from compounding errors, a lack of social compliance on sidewalks, and deficiencies in counterfactual reasoning to handle complex situations. To address these challenges, we introduce FlowPilot, a mapless navigation policy that achieves robust and efficient long-horizon navigation performance using only a monocular RGB camera. We first propose to use anchored flow matching as an action representation for policy pre-training on large-scale robot fleet data and to capture the diverse, complex, multimodal distribution of sidewalk navigation behaviors. To bridge the gap between imitation and alignment, we further design a human-in-the-loop preference learning scheme to tune the policy on a small amount of human intervention data. It strengthens the model's counterfactual reasoning and social compliance on sidewalks. We evaluate FlowPilot through extensive simulation and real-world experiments in diverse sidewalk environments. FlowPilot achieves 42% success rate and 66% route completion in simulation, while FlowPilot-HP further improves real-world robustness and social compliance, reducing IR by 40.0% and NIR by 52.1% relative to the base model. Code and model will be made available.
PaperID: 525,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.21201    
Authors:  Yu He, Da Huang, Zhenyang Liu, Zixiao Gu, Qiang Sun, Guangnan Ye, Yanwei Fu, Yu-Gang Jiang
Title: Schrödinger's Navigator: Imagining an Ensemble of Futures for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
Keywords: Robot navigation and locomotion
Abstract:
Zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) requires robots to find target objects in unseen environments without task-specific fine-tuning or pre-built maps, a key capability for general-purpose service robots. Yet methods that perform well in simulation often degrade in cluttered real-world scenes with severe occlusion and latent hazards, where large unseen regions make single-scene inference brittle and unsafe. We propose Schrödinger's Navigator, a belief-aware framework that reasons at inference time over multiple \emphtrajectory-conditioned imagined 3D futures. Given candidate paths, a trajectory-conditioned 3D world model predicts hypothetical observations and maintains a superposition of plausible scene realizations rather than committing to one map. An adaptive occluder-aware sampler directs imagination to uncertainty-critical regions, while a \emphFuture-Aware Value Map (FAVM) aggregates imagined futures for robust, proactive action selection. Experiments in simulation and on a physical Go2 quadruped show that Schrödinger's Navigator outperforms strong ZSON baselines, improving hidden-target discovery and risk-aware waypoint selection in occlusion-heavy navigation scenarios. These results highlight imagined 3D futures as a scalable and generalizable strategy for zero-shot navigation in uncertain real-world environments.
PaperID: 526,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.29881     GitHub
Authors:  Muxin Liu, TIANBO LIU, Jing Xia, Xiaoyang Lyu, Xiaoshan Wu, Bo Wang, Peng Dai, Zhongrui Wang, Shaoshuai Shi, Xiaojuan Qi
Title: OptiGeo: Efficient Monocular Geometry for Embodied Perception in Optically Challenging Scenes
Keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Monocular Depth Estimation
Abstract:
Monocular depth estimation has achieved strong open-domain generalization, yet reliable robotic deployment remains difficult in transparent, reflective, and specular environments, where depth sensors often produce missing or biased depth. Existing methods often handle such optical failures with scene-specific preprocessing, auxiliary modules, or post-hoc fine-tuning. While effective in constrained settings, these designs increase architectural redundancy and can over-specialize general geometry models to narrow optical scenarios. We revisit this problem as a localized failure mode within base-model training and identify sensor-induced supervision bias as a key bottleneck: models inherit sensor failure patterns from biased real-depth supervision in optically challenging regions. We then introduce OptiGeo, a bias-aware training framework that rehabilitates biased real supervision using a clean-geometry teacher and residual-trimmed alignment. We redefine transparency-targeted rendering as a compact source of clean optical geometry, rather than a large domain-specific fine-tuning set. With only a small targeted rendering set, OptiGeo learns the geometric structure of transparent objects and regions, correcting local geometry distortions that real sensors cannot reliably supervise. Despite only 30M parameters, OptiGeo outperforms substantially larger 300M-scale monocular models and billion-scale multi-view baselines on transparent-scene benchmarks, while remaining competitive on general zero-shot depth and boundary sharpness. Real-world navigation cases further validate its practicality as an efficient perception module in optically challenging scenes.
PaperID: 527,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Jonathan Hungerbühler, Felix Jahncke, Edoardo Ghignone, Maurice Brunner, Moritz Wagner, Andreas Blum, Andrea Carron, Johannes Betz, Michele Magno
Title: MaD-PF: Modular and Differentiable Particle Filter for Cross-Environment SE(3) LiDAR Localization
Keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Field Robotics, Differentiable Localization
Abstract:
Multi-modal robust localization requires estimating uncertainty over multiple pose hypotheses while adapting perception and motion models across environments and robotic platforms. Classical particle filters provide a principled Bayesian framework for this problem, but their manually specified models and discrete resampling operations limit integration into end-to-end trainable robotic systems, while learning-based localization approaches typically lack the modularity and generalizability. Differentiable particle filters promise to combine these two worlds by replacing filtering components with differentiable alternatives, but existing methods remain confined to either planar state spaces, visual or simulated observations, or single-platform evaluation. We present the first end-to-end differentiable particle filter capable of real-world cross-environment SE(3) LiDAR localization by using a unit dual quaternion formulation, 3D-LiDAR observations, and differentiable motion, observation, and resampling modules. Within this framework, we thoroughly compare different submodules and propose improvements that demonstrate increased robustness on held-out datasets and, in parallel, \qty89\percent latency reduction for the observation model. We evaluate the framework on real-world LiDAR data, demonstrating zero-shot RMSE of \qty0.398m or better in unknown environments, on different robotic platforms, or both, and we outperform SotA learning-based localization systems requiring 2.5 × less training time. Project Website: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/MaD-PF/
PaperID: 528,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Haoying Li, Qihang Liu, Yifan Peng, Keyan Miao, Junfeng Wu
Title: PLATO: Privileged Learning from Accurate Trajectory Observations for Neural Inertial Preintegration
Keywords: Probabilistic learning and uncertainty in robotics, Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision
Abstract:
Neural inertial odometry has demonstrated strong potential for motion estimation in challenging environments, yet inertial-only preintegration remains sensitive to IMU bias and uncertainty. To this end, this paper introduces PLATO:~\emphPrivileged Learning from Accurate Trajectory Observations, a likelihood-based framework that leverages accurate trajectory observations to jointly learn IMU bias dynamics modeled by a neural ordinary differential equation~(NODE) and gyroscope and accelerometer noise covariances. Optimization exploits the sparse structure of the negative log-likelihood, with IMU noise-parameter gradients computed by forward differentiation. A tailored double-adjoint scheme couples a discrete invariant-error adjoint with a continuous-time adjoint for the bias NODE, enabling memory-efficient likelihood optimization over the nested bias-dynamics and IMU-preintegration rollouts. Validation on EuRoC shows improved performance, and underwater robot experiments demonstrate applicability under intermittent lighting failures and visual degradation.
PaperID: 529,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Junyao Shi, Rujia Yang, Kaitian Chao, Bingqing Selina Wan, Yifei Simon Shao, Jiahui Lei, Jianing Qian, Long Le, Pratik Chaudhari, Kostas Daniilidis, Chuan Wen, Dinesh Jayaraman
Title: MAESTRO: Orchestrating Robotics Modules with Coding Agents for Zero-Shot Generalist Robots
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Robot manipulation, VLM coding agents for robot manipulation, Modular generalist manipulation
Abstract:
Today’s dominant route to generalist robots scales robotics data to train end-to-end policies. We instead use a vision-language model (VLM) as a coding agent that writes robot programs using a curated library of perception, planning, and control tools. MAESTRO’s orchestration harness packages multi-step perception and action procedures into callable tools and guides their use through a plan–act–replan loop, using visual and execution feedback to verify outcomes and recover from failures. With this tool library and harness, MAESTRO matches or surpasses state-of-the-art vision-language-action (VLA) models zero-shot in our tabletop comparison and performs diverse mobile manipulation tasks, without collecting new teleoperation data or invoking a VLA tool. Ablations show that expanding the tool library improves average task progress with the full harness, while adding tools without it does not reliably improve progress. Additional case studies examine cross-trial code improvement, VLA tool use, and autonomous seed demonstrations for downstream data augmentation. We argue that such agentic systems offer a complementary, far less-explored axis to data scaling for general-purpose robots. Project site: maestro-robot.github.io. Code: github.com/Beethoven-Q/maestro.
PaperID: 530,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.03132     GitHub
Authors:  Seunghwan Jang, Jeongyong Yang, Siddharth Ancha, SooJean Han
Title: Safe Streaming Flow Planning by Aligning Sampling Dynamics with Execution Dynamics
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems
Abstract:
Generative planners based on diffusion/flow matching can learn to synthesize long-horizon trajectories from demonstrations. However, real-world deployment requires (i) certified collision avoidance and (ii) tight online replanning at fast execution rates. Prior safe diffusion/flow planners generate the agent’s full trajectory at once, while repeatedly perturbing intermediate states to satisfy safety constraints. This approach is not only computationally intensive, but also introduces distribution shift since the learned sampling dynamics is distinct from the system’s execution dynamics. We propose SafeStreamingFlow, a goal-conditioned planner that aligns flow sampling dynamics with execution dynamics by sequentially integrating a learned state vector field. Importantly, we need to certify safety only for the executed step via high order control barrier functions. To improve robustness, we introduce a hierarchical network architecture that predicts the next position before predicting the next physical velocity. Across navigation, racing, and locomotion benchmarks, SafeStreamingFlow reduces planning latency and improves safety compared to existing methods, while main taining competitive goal-reaching success.
PaperID: 531,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.18606    
Authors:  Jixian Liu, Ihab Tabbara, Hussein Sibai, Enrique Mallada
Title: On the Limits of Sampling-Based Reachability: Geometry, Dynamics, and Sample Complexity
Keywords: Theoretical foundations of robot learning, Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems, Sampling-based reachable set approximation, Fundamental limits of sampling-based reachability
Abstract:
Reachability analysis is central to safety-critical control, robotics, and neural network verification, but classical computational methods, such as Hamilton--Jacobi reachability and set propagation, scale poorly with state dimension. Sampling-based methods have emerged as a promising alternative, often providing finite-sample guarantees that bound the probability-mass left uncovered. However, an explicit account of how the geometry of the initial set, the dynamics, and the sampling law affect the accuracy of the estimator is not fully available in the literature. We study this by casting sampling-based reachable-set recovery as geometric support estimation over a family of problems specified by an initial set, its dynamics, and a sampling law. First, we identify two regularity properties, positive reach of the initial set's complement and Lipschitz continuity of the dynamics, that together make recovery well-posed: a probability-mass coverage guarantee can be upgraded to accuracy r in Hausdorff distance. Second, we bound the resulting sample complexity: recovery is achievable with \tilde\mathcalO\!\big((e^3LT/r)^n\big) samples, exponential in both the state dimension and the time horizon. Third, we show that neither can be removed: an almost-matching minimax lower bound of \Omega\!\big((e^LT/r)^n\big) holds for every estimator, so the exponential dependence on dimension and the degradation over the horizon are both intrinsic, not artifacts of a particular method. Experiments on nonlinear systems confirm that adversarial sampling improves constants but not the scaling.
PaperID: 532,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.26408    
Authors:  Phone Thiha Kyaw, Miguel Rogel-García, Jonathan Kelly
Title: Exploring the Intrinsic Geometry of Diffusion Models with Constrained Inverse Kinematics
Keywords: Theoretical foundations of robot learning, Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Generative Models for Robotics, Constrained Inverse Kinematics
Abstract:
Recent studies suggest that diffusion models can recover geometric structure in the data manifolds they are trained on, yet the supporting evidence has so far come mostly from natural-image data, where the underlying geometry itself is unknown. We study this question in a setting where the geometry is analytically tractable: constrained inverse kinematics (IK). Each task-space constraint defines a configuration-space manifold with known intrinsic dimension, giving direct ground truth for evaluating the geometry learned by the model. For each of the 6-DoF UR5 and 7-DoF Franka, we train a single conditional diffusion model across seven constraint families, spanning solution manifolds from discrete IK branches to self-motion manifolds. Our empirical results reveal that the intrinsic dimension recovered from the model's score function matches the analytical degrees of freedom of the corresponding constraint manifold across both robots. Moreover, linear interpolation in the latent space leads to generated solutions that remain close to the appropriate constraint manifold, indicating that the learned representation further captures geometric structure of the constraint family beyond intrinsic dimension alone. Constrained IK therefore offers a controlled setting for studying the intrinsic geometry learned by diffusion models.
PaperID: 533,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.15550     GitHub GitHub
Authors:  RUOFEI BAI, Jie Chen, Yuxin Cai, Li jun, Wei-Yun Yau, Lihua Xie
Title: Robots as Tokens: Unified Diffusion Transformer for Coordinated Multi-Robot Trajectory Generation
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)
Abstract:
The success of generative models in language, image, and video generation has inspired extensive applications to generative robot planning. However, most existing works either focus on single-robot planning, or generate multi-robot trajectories in a sequential manner with iterative post-processing to resolve inter-robot conflicts. In this work, we investigate whether coordinated multi-robot trajectories, as a special spatiotemporal distribution, can be learned and generated with a generative model in a feed-forward manner. We propose Robots as Tokens (Roken), a unified diffusion transformer that directly generates multi-robot trajectories that satisfy both (individual) safety and (global) connectivity constraints. The core design of Roken is to represent each robot as a discrete token, allowing them to naturally interact with each other through self-attention, and cross-attend to map tokens for environment layouts. We further introduce several auxiliary tasks based on Bayes' theorem, specifically local occupancy reconstruction and long-horizon waypoint prediction, to provide multi-scale spatial-temporal supervision for efficient learning of the conditional distribution. In training, Roken absorbs diverse expert trajectories from different team sizes. During inference, Roken behaves as a versatile multi-robot planner that can handle single-robot planning, coordinated multi-robot trajectory generation, and conditional trajectory generation by fixing some robot tokens as conditions. Experiments in diverse cluttered environments show that Roken can generate coordinated multi-robot trajectories to perform connectivity-constrained goal navigation tasks with high success rates, outperforming the baseline method used to generate the training dataset. Roken also demonstrates good scalability after training with mixed team sizes, and shows generalization to unseen or partially observed environments, verifying its potential as a unified multi-robot planner that can learn from diverse data and perform versatile tasks.
PaperID: 534,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Zongyao Lyu, Lingling Chen, William J. Beksi
Title: SentryVLA: Uncertainty-Guided Action Selection and State Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Robotic Control
Keywords: Probabilistic learning and uncertainty in robotics
Abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as generalist robotic controllers that map visual observations and language instructions to continuous actions. However, pretrained VLAs typically provide limited information about the reliability of their generated actions, making deployment challenging when execution failures must be anticipated. We introduce SentryVLA, a lightweight runtime wrapper for frozen VLA policies. At the action level, SentryVLA uses conformalized quantile regression to estimate a calibrated upper bound on the predicted deviation between sampled VLA actions and expert-like behavior under the calibration distribution. This score is used to select, among multiple stochastic action candidates, the action with the lowest estimated execution risk. At the execution-monitoring level, SentryVLA applies a Mahalanobis-distance-based anomaly score to the contextualized latent execution state extracted before final action prediction, providing a complementary signal for detecting abnormal execution states during closed-loop control. The framework does not require retraining or architectural modification of the underlying VLA policy. Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot show that SentryVLA improves action selection and provides useful runtime warning signals for abnormal execution states. These findings demonstrate the practical value of post-hoc reliability scoring for improving the runtime behavior of pretrained VLA policies.
PaperID: 535,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Negin Musavi, Gokul Puthumanaillam, Ruben Hernandez, William Schafer, Melkior Ornik
Title: When Should a Robot Replan? Regret-Guided Update Scheduling in Time-Varying MDPs
Keywords: Model-based and model-free learning for robotic control, Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Theoretical foundations of robot learning
Abstract:
Robots operating in non-stationary environments must continually adapt their policies as the dynamics drift, but onboard energy and compute budgets cap how often a full state estimation and re-planning step can be performed. This raises a question: \emphwhen, along a horizon, should a robot spend its limited budget? We formulate this problem in time-varying Markov decision processes (TVMDPs) with a known bound on the rate of transition drift. We model execution as a \emphskip-update scheme in which, at chosen update times, the agent estimates the transition kernel by maximum likelihood and computes a finite-horizon policy, and between updates reuses this policy under a propagated state estimate. We analyze the dynamic regret of this scheme and show how it grows during skip intervals in terms of the properties of the TVMDP and the skip lengths; the resulting bound answers the opening question via an online, regret-guided update rule that allocates the budget adaptively. We evaluate the rule in a simulated Mars-rover navigation task with time-varying slip dynamics and on a Crazyflie quadrotor in indoor obstacle fields. Adaptive allocation outperforms other budgeted baselines.

Authors:  Xiaopeng Zhang, Mu Yongjin, Yueyang Weng, Chengzhi zhao, Yanjie Li
Title: W2A: Distilling World Priors into Action Models for Real-Time Robotic Control
Keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Robot manipulation, World Action Model, Distillation
Abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) have recently shown great promise in robotic control, benefiting from the future imagination capability of large-scale pretrained video models. However, most existing WAMs require explicitly imagining future states at test time, incurring substantial computational overhead and latency that make them unsuitable for real-time robotic control. In this paper, we propose W2A, a two-stage distillation framework for real-time robotic manipulation that distills intermediate denoising representations from a video diffusion model into an action model during training, while entirely discarding the video model at test time. We hypothesize that although video latent representations are high-dimensional, a compressed low-dimensional subspace is sufficient to provide effective supervision for action generation. This makes it possible to transfer such information effectively into an action model. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate competitive success rates while significantly improving inference efficiency. On LIBERO, W2A achieves a 95.9% average success rate. More importantly, W2A achieves about 21X faster inference than the representative WAM baseline. Project website: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/W2A.
PaperID: 537,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.21022    
Authors:  Yiheng Ji, Xingru Zhou, Luis Sentis, Mingyo Seo
Title: Catch Me If You Can: Real-Time Feedback Denoising for Responsive VLAs
Keywords: Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by combining semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models with expressive action-generation policies. Diffusion-based action generators are particularly effective for modeling temporally coherent action chunks, but these chunks are typically executed open-loop after inference. This limits responsiveness when objects move, contacts change, or the scene evolves during execution. We propose VLA-Feedback, a two-timescale architecture that combines low-frequency diffusion planning with high-frequency observation feedback. Rather than fully denoising an action chunk before execution, VLA-Feedback stops before the final denoising stage and refines the chunk online using observation-conditioned denoising velocity updates at control frequency. This design preserves the expressiveness of the diffusion planner while enabling real-time action correction without rerunning the full vision-language diffusion model. Experiments on stationary and non-stationary manipulation tasks show that VLA-Feedback preserves static-task performance while improving robustness in dynamic environments.
PaperID: 538,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.22836    
Authors:  Michael Piseno, Guy Tevet, Karen Liu
Title: Cloak: Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment Manipulation by Masking the End-Effector from the VLA
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
Abstract:
We present Cloak, a training recipe that endows a vision-language-action policy with zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer by cloaking the end-effector from its own wrist camera. The mask comes for free from the robot's geometry and camera calibration, projected into the wrist view in real time with no generative model and nothing to hallucinate, and is augmented during training so the policy does not overfit to the end-effector's geometry. At deployment, we mask an unseen end-effector the same way and retarget its state and actions through two tips, the gripper jaws or a hand's fingertips, by inverse kinematics. We demonstrate the recipe with Cloak-VLA, fine-tuned on a single parallel-jaw gripper. Without new data or retraining, it transfers zero-shot to end-effectors it never saw, from another gripper to a five-fingered dexterous hand, at little cost to its performance on the source. Masking the wrist view is what unlocks this transfer: strong baselines given the same retargeting but no mask collapse on the unseen embodiments, most sharply on the dexterous hand.
PaperID: 539,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Mingyu Liu, Zeju Li, Jiuhe Shu, Hanqing Wang, Yuhao Chao, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
Title: Perfect Demo Makes Poor Teacher:Learning Robust Alignment from Critical Motion Segments
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)
Abstract:
Expert demonstrations are often assumed to be the gold standard for robot imitation learning, yet for fine-grained manipulation tasks such as insertion, stacking, and alignment, we find a counterintuitive failure mode: fluent expert demonstrations can be poor teachers. Skilled teleoperators compress the most critical alignment and recovery behaviors into a brief temporal window, leaving imitation models dominated by redundant free-space motion and starved of supervision on the high-precision segments that actually determine success. We study this phenomenon through the lens of critical motion segments and propose three complementary remedies: (i) a deliberate demonstration strategy that slows down near alignment and exposes corrective micro-adjustments, (ii) a resampling scheme that upweights key segments around gripper state changes and task-critical transitions, and (iii) a dynamic feature representation that compresses short temporal neighborhoods of visual observations into predictive features, conditioning the action expert on local motion and alignment progress rather than isolated static frames. Together, these results show that robust robotic alignment benefits less from perfect trajectories than from demonstrations and representations that expose the structure of correction, pointing toward a more pedagogical view of robot data collection where demonstrations are optimized not only for human efficiency but for machine learnability.
PaperID: 540,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.12433     GitHub GitHub
Authors:  Yuxing Chen, Zhiyuan Wei, Bowen Xiao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
Title: FoldNet++: a Large-Scale Synthetic Dataset for Robotic T-Shirt Folding and Unfolding
Keywords: Robotic data generation, Sim-to-real transfer, Deformable object manipulation, Datasets for robot learning
Abstract:
Due to the highly deformable nature of garments, training a generalizable policy for robotic T-shirt folding and unfolding remains a significant challenge. In this work, we present a large-scale synthetic dataset for robotic T-shirt folding and unfolding, covering 6 robotic embodiments, 1K T-shirts, 1K environmental assets, and 120K episodes with rich annotations, which can be used to train a wide range of manipulation policies. We first follow the FoldNet pipeline to generate a large-scale dataset of physically simulatable T-shirts with diverse appearances and annotated semantic keypoints. Based on these semantic keypoints, we then generate manipulation demonstrations for different robotic embodiments through a unified rule-based framework. We use these demonstrations to train visuomotor policies, and experimental results demonstrate that models trained solely on our synthetic data can achieve over 90% end-to-end task success rates when directly deployed to unseen real-world environments and previously unseen T-shirts from arbitrary initial configurations.

Authors:  Zhiyuan Xiang, Peidong Liu, Mingyang Li, Jiawei Li, Wenhow Li, Wenbo Ding, Xiang Deng
Title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Latent action learning from human videos for robot policy pre-training, Scaling robot policies with human-video supervision
Abstract:
Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours.
PaperID: 542,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.08436     GitHub GitHub
Authors:  Baoyu Li, Xinchen Yin, Mengying Lin, Yixin Zhang, Danfei Xu
Title: EgoWAM: World Action Models Beyond Pixels with In-the-Wild Egocentric Human Data
Keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Learning from Human Data, Robot Manipulation
Abstract:
Egocentric human data offers scalable supervision for robot manipulation. However, behavior cloning entangles transferable content like objects, scenes, and task semantics, with non-transferable factors like human morphology, head motion, and behavioral style. We study whether World Action Models (WAMs) provide a better training signal by requiring policies to predict not only actions, but also how the scene evolves. The central question is what world representation best enables human-to-robot transfer. We hypothesize that an effective world target should abstract appearance, capture agent-invariant physical effects, and separate camera motion from environment change. We introduce EgoWAM, a controlled human-robot co-training framework that fixes the policy backbone, action head, and data mixture while varying only the world prediction target, comparing Pixel, DINO, and 3D motion flow. Across three real-world bimanual tasks, WAM co-training scales more effectively with in-the-wild egocentric human data than behavior cloning. Pixel-based prediction transfers weakly, while DINO and 3D flow yield substantial gains: DINO improves out-of-distribution object and scene generalization by up to 4×, and 3D flow improves in-domain performance by 20–30%. More details: https://egowam.github.io/.
PaperID: 543,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Filippo Lazzati, Kyle Stachowicz, William Chen, Alberto Maria Metelli, Andrew Wagenmaker, Sergey Levine
Title: Why Does Action Chunking Improve Behavioral Cloning Performance in Robotic Control?
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Theoretical foundations of robot learning, Action Chunking
Abstract:
Action chunking---predicting and executing multiple future actions instead of a single action---has proven to be a critical component for learning effective robotic control policies. However, our precise understanding of \emphwhy action chunking improves performance has remained limited. In this work we seek to close this gap. Through rigorous experimental evaluations, we first show that, while existing hypotheses for the success of action chunking---in particular non-Markovian expressivity, horizon reduction, and representation learning---can each partially explain the success of action chunking, in many settings of interest \emphdelayed policies, which at each step predict a single action based on the state k steps in the past, can match or exceed the performance of action chunking, fully accounting for the benefits of these hypotheses. We then show that there exists an additional benefit of action chunking not accounted for previously that we refer to as \emphimplicit ensembling. In particular, by learning a diversity of temporal relationships (that is, a_t | o_t, a_t | o_t-1, \ldots), action-chunked policies exhibit behavior matching that of a model ensemble, increasing their robustness and generalization ability over policies that only learn a \emphsingle temporal relationship. Motivated by these findings, we propose a policy class that amplifies this effect of action chunking by explicitly instantiating an ensemble, and which we show significantly improves over the performance of action chunking in many domains.

Authors:  Hao Wang, Jiuzhou Lei, Dayou Li, Bangya Liu, Minghui Zheng, Manling Li, Ruohan Zhang, Zhiwen Fan
Title: Behavior Uncloning: Distilling Mode Redirection into Policy Weights without Inference-Time Steering
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Learning representations for robotic perception and control
Abstract:
Behavior-cloned policies often learn multiple behavior modes from demonstration datasets, including modes that are unsafe or otherwise undesired at deployment. For example, a policy trained on diverse handover demonstrations may learn to pass a knife blade-first. Standard remedies such as data curation and inference-time steering either require access to the original demonstrations for full retraining or add substantial inference-time overhead. To address this gap, we propose MoRE (Mode Redirection), which redirects policy rollouts toward desired behavior modes through a short "uncloning" step. Specifically, MoRE distills the redirection signal from a temporary mode classifier into the policy weights to steer behavior. A retain loss balances this edit by preserving desired-mode competence, allowing the standalone policy to suppress unwanted modes with zero inference-time overhead. Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, MoRE improves average deployment success rate (SR) by 43 percentage points over the original mixed-mode policy. Among all compared adaptation and steering baselines, MoRE achieves the strongest SR and approaches the filtered-data retraining reference, while preserving task competence and inference speed. MoRE also generalizes across robot policy backbones, including Diffusion Policy and the \pi_0.5 VLA, diverse task categories, and real-world deployments.

Authors:  Kaneyoshi Hiratsuka, Benjamin Yen, Ryosuke Kojima
Title: S2A2: Audio-Visual Imitation Learning for Manipulation Tasks Using Acoustic Spatial Information
Keywords: Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Robot manipulation, Robot Audition, Sound Source Localization
Abstract:
Acoustic information provides rich cues about object location, material properties, and changes caused by contact or motion. This paper introduces a new set of acoustic-aware manipulation tasks for imitation learning, in which robots must use auditory cues to determine manipulation targets. These tasks require sound source localization and identification for active exploration in robotic manipulation. Also, we propose a multimodal imitation learning framework, Spatial-Spectral Audio Action (S2A2), that integrates visual features with acoustic spatial and acoustic signal information for the acoustic-aware manipulation tasks. We implemented S2A2 models that integrates policies such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, VQ-BeT, and \pi_0, into our framework. Simulation experiments showed that the proposed method is the most effective for tasks requiring both position and timbre. Furthermore, real-robot experiments confirm the applicability of the proposed tasks and framework to real-world manipulation.

Authors:  Wenhao Li, Dong Li, Zhihua Xie, Wenbo Li
Title: RAMT-VLA: Reliability-Aware Memory Tracing for Historical Support Assessment in Vision-Language-Action Models
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
Abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are effective generalist robot controllers, but in long-horizon tasks a visually plausible action can be inappropriate unless earlier subgoals have been completed. We introduce historical support, a reliability criterion asking whether task history justifies a candidate action at the current decision step. Based on this criterion, RAMT-VLA keeps the base VLA frozen and adds a lightweight post-policy assessor that scores candidate action chunks, outputs sparse evidence masks for each candidate, and reranks candidates by historical support. The assessor is trained without dense evidence annotations using wrong-history and missing-evidence counterfactuals, with sparsity and faithfulness regularization. With a frozen 0.5B base model, RAMT-VLA achieves 98.1% average success on LIBERO, 83.3% on SimplerEnv-WidowX, and 84.0% on real-world long-horizon tasks. Matched LIBERO ablations, candidate-selection controls, and transfer evaluations show that support-based reranking improves the frozen base policy, with the largest history-dependent gains on long-horizon tasks, beyond generic sampling or policy-confidence reranking.
PaperID: 547,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Haoran Wang, Jingwei Huang, Anqing Duan, Ho Seok Ahn, Bruce A. MacDonald
Title: HelpMeOut: A Neuropsychology-Grounded Benchmark for Error-Aware Monitoring of Household Task Execution
Keywords: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning, Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction, Assistive Robotics, Error-Aware Monitoring
Abstract:
We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, \textscHelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20,000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate supervised sequence models and LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.

Authors:  Ayush Kaura, Vignesh Vembar, Md Faizal Karim, Keshab Patra, Madhava Krishna
Title: PartialBiGrasp: Inferring Hidden Local Geometry for Bimanual Grasping from Partial Views
Keywords: Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Dual-arm robotic grasping is essential for manipulating large, heavy, and geometrically complex objects that cannot be reliably handled using a single manipulator. These large objects often contain only sparse graspable regions determined by local geometric properties such as thickness, edge structure, and gripper clearance. Prior bimanual grasping methods assume access to a full point cloud of the object which inherently contains this geometric information, but may not be accessible in real scenarios. This work proposes PartialBiGrasp, a dual-arm grasp generation framework that operates directly on partial point cloud observations.Our model learns geometric features implicitly through convolutional occupancy networks, enabling local reasoning about graspability, collision-free contact regions, and object thickness. We leverage this understanding to generate force-closure compliant grasp pairs, which are further refined using a sampling-based optimization to correct for ambiguity caused by incomplete geometry. We evaluate our approach using analytical force-closure metrics, large-scale simulation experiments, and real-world testing on noisy point clouds of novel objects, demonstrating robust and physically stable dual-arm grasp generation for large-object manipulation under partial observations.
