This forces reconstruction gradients to pass exclusively through the scene-token bottleneck, encouraging scene tokens to preserve richer and less redundant visual representations for planning. We further introduce semantic priors derived from foundation-model annotations as a weak semantic interface biasing reconstruction targets toward driving-related structures without introducing explicit perception heads. All auxiliary reconstruction components are removed at inference time, leaving the deployed planner unchanged. NTR achieves state-of-the-art performance on three public autonomous driving benchmarks, including 8.0461 RFS on Waymo E2E and 94.1 PDMS / 90.9 EPDMS on NavSim1&2. The learned scene tokens exhibit lower pairwise redundancy and higher effective rank, indicating that effective bottleneck supervision improves both compact visual representation learning and planning performance. We further validate NTR on a private large-scale driving dataset and integrate it into a real-vehicle planning stack, demonstrating its practical applicability beyond public benchmarks. Real-world deployment videos are provided in the supplementary materials.
PaperID: 594,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.03678    
Authors:  Tong Nie, Yuewen Mei, Yihong Tang, Junlin He, Jie Deng, Jian Sun, Wei Ma
Title: EvoDrive: Pareto Evolution for Safety-Critical Autonomous Driving via Self-Improving LLM Agents
Keywords: Autonomous driving and flight, Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming
Abstract:
Generating safety-critical scenarios is essential for validating and improving autonomous driving systems, yet it inherently requires maximizing adversariality to expose failures while preserving realism. Existing methods usually manage this trade-off with handcrafted heuristics, confining generation to known priors and overlooking underexplored patterns. While recent open-ended agentic evolution can push this limit, unconstrained general agents lack strict simulator grounding and tend to collapse the multi-objective tension into single-scalar maximization. Here we present EvoDrive, the first automated, LLM-based agentic evolution framework for multi-objective scenario generation. EvoDrive employs a simulator-grounded actor-critic architecture where a memory-driven actor iteratively proposes improvements to the generators and critics filter out implausible candidates, and a self-evolving world evaluator routes promising proposals to optimize simulation budgets. EvoDrive further maintains a Pareto archive of evaluated candidates to preserve diverse attack-realism trade-offs and guide future evolution via simulation feedback. Benchmark results on MetaDrive and CARLA show that EvoDrive not only significantly expands the Pareto frontier across various generators, but also produces valuable scenarios for policy training.
PaperID: 595,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Zhenyu Zong, Yuchen Wang, Jiangtao Kong, Xiaochang Li, Lui Sha, Huajie Shao
Title: An Adaptive Slow-Fast Framework for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Autonomous Driving
Keywords: Autonomous driving and flight, Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning, Anomaly Detection
Abstract:
Anomaly detection is essential for ensuring the safety and reliability of autonomous driving systems operating in open environments, where rare objects, abnormal behaviors, and long-tail events frequently arise. Conventional perception-based approaches often lack the contextual understanding necessary to interpret complex anomalies, while recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods incur substantial computational overhead and exhibit limited integration with geometric sensory modalities. To address these challenges, we propose SOFA, an adaptive slow-fast anomaly detection and reasoning framework that selectively activates multimodal reasoning only when anomalous events are detected. SOFA integrates three key components: 1) a fast LiDAR-based anomaly detection module for efficient real-time perception, 2) a slow VLM-based reasoning module for semantic understanding, and 3) a Time-to-Collision (TTC)-driven switching mechanism that dynamically coordinates the two modules to balance efficiency and reasoning fidelity. To enable systematic evaluation of multimodal anomaly detection and reasoning in real-world driving scenarios, we further construct MAQA, a Multimodal Anomaly Question Answering dataset comprising 16K anomalous objects, synchronized LiDAR-image observations, and reasoning-oriented language annotations. Extensive experiments on MAQA demonstrate that SOFA significantly outperforms baselines in detection accuracy, computational efficiency, and reasoning capability.
PaperID: 596,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.03693    
Authors:  Haozhe Zhang, Sixian Li, Yifei Zhang, Zezheng Huai, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen, Jingjing Gong, Xipeng Qiu
Title: CoRE-VLA: Towards Scalable and Robust Vision-Language-Action Modeling via Conditional Routing of Experts
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced generalist robotic manipulation, yet real-world deployment reveals a fundamental challenge: robots are equipped with diverse and heterogeneous sensor configurations, auxiliary sensors can fail unexpectedly during operation, and different robot embodiments often lack certain sensors by design. A unified policy that can exploit auxiliary perceptual inputs when available while remaining reliable under sensor absence — whether incidental or by design — is therefore essential for practical deployment. However, existing VLA policies couple action generation to a fixed sensor set through shared dense computation, making them brittle when sensors are missing and limiting their ability to specialize across diverse tasks and long-horizon behaviors. We propose CoRE-VLA, a scalable and robust VLA framework that formulates action generation as context-conditioned sparse computation. Sensor availability gates modality-specialized experts, enabling graceful degradation under missing sensors without retraining. Task intent further routes action-side representations to task-relevant experts, improving specialization across diverse tasks and long-horizon subgoals. While the framework is designed to accommodate different auxiliary sensors, we focus on depth as a representative and practically important auxiliary modality in our experiments. Experiments on LIBERO, RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop, and real-world dual-arm manipulation show that CoRE-VLA achieves strong results on long-horizon and multi-task benchmarks, and outperforms both a dense-action-generator ablation and a strong pretrained VLA baseline, including in zero-shot generalization to unseen scenarios. Modality analysis shows that CoRE-VLA can exploit auxiliary depth when available while remaining robust when depth is unavailable during deployment.
PaperID: 597,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.21139     GitHub
Authors:  Youngjoon Jeong, Jihwan Yu, Minsoo Jo, Junha Chun, Taesup Kim
Title: PoLAR: Factorizing Extent and Mode in Latent Actions for Robot Policy Learning
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Latent Actions
Abstract:
Latent action pretraining learns representations of visual change from pairs of observations, but existing methods typically encode each transition as a single unstructured representation that entangles transition extent and transition mode. We introduce Polar Latent Actions with Radial structure (PoLAR), which imposes a radial-direction structure on latent actions, encouraging radius to encode transition extent and direction to retain transition mode. PoLAR uses temporal offset between two observations as a weak proxy for transition extent, encouraging latent action from observation pairs separated by larger temporal gaps to occupy larger radii. We instantiate this structure in hyperbolic space, whose expanding volume with radius offers a natural fit for more diverse transition modes at larger extents. Across in-task and large-scale pretraining settings, PoLAR improves downstream policy performance in simulation and real-world robot experiments, outperforming latent action baselines and strong pretrained VLAs. These results suggest that the geometry of the latent action space is an important design choice for transferring visual pretraining to downstream robot policy learning.
PaperID: 598,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03280     GitHub
Authors:  Toru Lin, Shuying Deng, Zhao-Heng Yin, Pieter Abbeel, Jitendra Malik
Title: How to Peel with a Knife: Aligning Fine-Grained Manipulation with Human Preference
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Learning from Human Preference
Abstract:
Many essential manipulation tasks -- such as food preparation, surgery, and craftsmanship -- remain difficult for autonomous robots. These tasks are characterized not only by contact-rich, force-sensitive dynamics, but also by their "implicit" success criteria: unlike pick-and-place, task quality in these domains is continuous and subjective (e.g. how well a potato is peeled), making quantitative evaluation and reward design difficult. We present a learning framework for such tasks, using peeling with a knife as a representative example. Our approach follows a two-stage pipeline: first, we learn a robust initial policy via force-aware data collection and imitation learning, enabling generalization across object variations; second, we refine the policy through preference-based finetuning using a learned reward model that combines quantitative task metrics with qualitative human feedback, aligning policy behavior with human notions of task quality. Using only 50--200 peeling trajectories, our system achieves 100% same-produce success on cucumbers, apples, and potatoes, with performance improving by up to 40% through preference-based finetuning. Remarkably, policies trained on one produce category also transfer zero-shot to selected held-out produce categories, achieving 50% success on zucchini, 90% on pear, and 80% on daikon radish.
PaperID: 599,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.13982    
Authors:  Qiping Zhang, Kate Candon, Debasmita Ghose, Marynel Vázquez
Title: Rethinking the Implications of Human Feedback for Preference Learning in Human-Robot Collaboration
Keywords: Human-robot interaction and natural language instruction, Explicit and Implicit Human Feedback, Interactive Learning
Abstract:
In Human-Robot Interaction, the standard approach to learn a reward model that represents human preferences for robot behavior consists of three steps. First, the robot collects limited direct evidence from human feedback (e.g., positive or negative binary feedback). Then, the robot utilizes the direct evidence to derive accepted or rejected labels to feasible but unchosen actions using fixed implication rules. Finally, the robot updates the reward model with both the direct and derived evidence. Unfortunately, the fixed rule can hinder preference learning: in a user study with two collaborative simulation environments, human-provided implication labels often differed from the standard fixed rule, and using the human labels substantially improved reward learning with the Preference Learning from Implicit and Explicit Feedback (PIE) algorithm. Consequently, we propose IMPLIED, an implication modeling method that treats fixed-rule implications as an initial guide while learning to infer and revise accepted and rejected action labels over time. Across evaluations on recorded human-robot interaction trajectories and a physical robot pizza-making study, IMPLIED predicts human implications more accurately than the fixed rule approach and LLM baselines, approaching the performance of a human-label oracle. In turn, IMPLIED reduces preference-estimation error and leads to robot actions that are more often rational with respect to a combined reward (which includes the true preference reward and a task-specific reward) compared to baselines. By learning to reason about the implications of human feedback, this work enables more faithful and efficient robot behavior adaptation during human-robot collaboration.
PaperID: 600,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Wenke Xia, Pei Ren, Wenbo Yu, Yizhuo Zhang, Jifan Li, Yixue Zhang, Yinuo Zhao, Qingyang Gao, Jianlong Fu, Jian Tang, Ji-Rong Wen, Zhengping Che, Di Hu
Title: Not All Actions are Equal: Reliable Value Estimation for Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot manipulation, Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
Abstract:
Offline-to-online reinforcement learning is a promising paradigm for generalizable robotic manipulation, but its full-stack complexity makes system behavior difficult to reproduce and diagnose. Within such systems, value estimation plays a central role by determining how heterogeneous data are prioritized for policy improvement. Despite its importance, a central question remains underexplored: how value-function reliability affects value-guided learning across offline pretraining and online adaptation. To answer this question, we ground our analysis in a complete offline-to-online reinforcement learning pipeline and introduce value-reliability metrics that quantify value-function quality along global task-level progress and local action-level preference, enabling us to analyze how value estimation affects downstream policy behavior. Across the extensive empirical study encompassing 240 hours of pretraining data and over 3,000 rollout trajectories, our experiments show that these metrics are closely aligned with downstream performance: More reliable value functions yield better action-quality estimates, enabling value-guided offline RL to scale more effectively than quality-agnostic behavior cloning. As value estimates become more reliable, online adaptation becomes more stable through better prioritization of high-quality rollout data. Integrating reliable value guidance through offline pretraining with online adaptation, our system achieves 86% success on millimeter-level precise chip insertion and 84% on generalizable block disassembly. Ultimately, we hope our findings could underscore the importance of value-guided data utilization for turning heterogeneous robotic experience into effective policy improvement. We will release the full offline-to-online RL framework and the corresponding pretraining data to promote reproducibility and further research.
PaperID: 601,   Poster  OpenReview   GitHub
Authors:  Marc Heim, Bassam Helou, Rohit Satishkumar, Momchil Tomov, Hansford C. Hendargo, Nicolas Rey, Gianmarco Bernasconi, Joseph Baker, Alexander Boule, Rafael DaSilva, Abed Ghanbari, Cedric Warny, Yi Huo, Phuc Xuan Nguyen, Neset Unver Akmandor, Sarjak Thakkar, Daphne Cornelisse, Eugene Vinitsky, Forbes Howington, Boaz Floor, Yiluan Guo, Samuel Findler, Sourabh Vora
Title: Self-play is not enough: human imitation improves self-play autonomy in the wild
Keywords: Autonomous driving and flight, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Self-play reinforcement learning, Sim-to-real transfer
Abstract:
Self-play reinforcement learning at scale has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training autonomous driving policies, producing agents that exhibit robust collision-avoidance and stable navigation in simulation. However, policies trained purely through self-play lack exposure to the distribution of real human driving behavior, resulting in trajectories that appear unnatural. To overcome this, we present Self-play with Human Imitation Fine-Tuning (SHIFT), a hybrid training framework that fine-tunes a pretrained self-play foundation policy on real-world driving demonstrations without changing the underlying reinforcement learning algorithm. SHIFT fine-tunes in closed-loop log-replay simulation, in which the ego vehicle is rolled out by the learned policy while the non-ego agents are replayed from logged human trajectories. Distance to the human expert trajectory is simply an additional reward term in the same PPO with advantage filtering algorithm used for pretraining. To enable extended fine-tuning without losing the base self-play performance, we use a KL regularization loss against the frozen self-play foundation policy. On the closed-loop nuPlan Val14 benchmark, SHIFT improves over the self-play baseline in human-likeness (ADE: 9.4 m → 8.0 m, FDE: 21.3 m → 18.5 m), safety (collision rate: 6.4% → 3.9%, drivable area violations: 2.5% → 1.7%, red light violations: 1.6% → 1.0%), and comfort (brake tap rate: 29% → 20%, oscillation rate: 9% → 4%), and achieves the best ADE, FDE, collision, and drivable area scores among all baselines, including extended self-play, behavior cloning, BC+RL, and human-regularized PPO. We deploy both policies on self-driving cars and find similar improvements in the real world (2.6× fewer safety takeovers: one every 0.57 → 1.46 miles). To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of self-play and self-play with human imitation on public roads. Our results suggest that post-training self-play with human imitation, stabilized by KL regularization, is a promising direction for deployable autonomous driving systems. An open-source implementation, along with additional materials, will be available on the project page: https://rohit-ash.github.io/SHIFT/
PaperID: 602,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Zhefei Gong, Hefeifei Jiang, Zehao Wang, Jiachen Li
Title: Hierarchical Residual Policy Learning for Real-World Mobile Manipulation with Sparse Human Guidance
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot manipulation, Real-world reinforcement learning, Human-robot interaction
Abstract:
Abstract: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning of such tasks remains a formidable challenge due to their high-dimensional action spaces and the intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform’s physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we integrate Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic’s value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Code and videos are available in the supplement.
PaperID: 603,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.13476    
Authors:  Noriaki Hirose, Catherine Glossop, Dhruv Shah, Sergey Levine
Title: AsyncVLA: An Asynchronous VLA for Fast and Robust Navigation on the Edge
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Robot navigation and locomotion
Abstract:
Robotic foundation models achieve strong generalization by leveraging internet-scale vision-language representations, but their massive computational cost creates a fundamental bottleneck: high inference latency. In dynamic environments, this latency breaks the control loop, rendering powerful models unsafe for real-time deployment. We propose AsyncVLA, an asynchronous control framework that decouples semantic reasoning from reactive execution. Inspired by hierarchical control, AsyncVLA runs a large foundation model on a remote workstation to provide high-level guidance, while a lightweight, onboard Edge Adapter continuously refines actions at high frequency. To bridge the domain gap between these asynchronous streams, we introduce an end-to-end finetuning protocol and a trajectory re-weighting strategy that prioritizes dynamic interactions. We evaluate our approach on real-world vision-based navigation tasks with communication delays up to 6 seconds. AsyncVLA achieves a 40% higher success rate than state-of-the-art baselines, effectively bridging the gap between the semantic intelligence of large models and the reactivity required for edge robotics.
PaperID: 604,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.07496    
Authors:  Yijin Wang, Yuru Tian, Xijie Huang, Weiqi Gai, Mo Zhu, Xin Zhou, Yuze Wu, Fei Gao
Title: PathPainter: Transferring the Generalization Ability of Image Generation Models to Embodied Navigation
Keywords: Robot navigation and locomotion
Abstract:
Bird's-eye-view (BEV) images have been widely demonstrated to provide valuable prior information for navigation. Given the global information provided by such views, two key challenges remain: how to fully exploit this information and how to reliably use it during execution. In this paper, we propose a navigation system that uses BEV images as global priors and is designed for ground and near-ground robotic platforms. The system employs an image generation model to interpret human intent from natural language, identify the target destination, and generate traversability masks. During execution, we introduce cross-view localization to align the robot's odometry with the BEV map and mitigate long-term drift in conventional odometry. We conduct extensive benchmark experiments to evaluate the proposed method and further validate it on both quadruped robot and UAV platforms. Using only a conventional local motion planner, the robot successfully completes a 285-meter outdoor long-range navigation task. This work demonstrates how the world-understanding capabilities of foundation models can be transferred to embodied navigation, enabling robots to benefit from the strong generalization ability of existing image generation models.
PaperID: 605,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20216     GitHub
Authors:  Haebin Seong, Sungmin Kim, Yongjun Cho, Myunchul Joe, Geunwoo Kim, Yu Been Park, Sunhoo Kim, Samwoo Seong, Yoonshik Kim, Suhwan Choi, Jaeyoon Jung, Jiyong Youn, Jin Myung Kwak, Sunghee Ahn, Jaemin Lee, Younggil Do, Seungyeop Yi, Woojin Cheong, Minhyeok Oh, Minchan Kim, Seongjae Kang, Youngjae Yu, Yunsung Lee
Title: CostNav: A Navigation Benchmark for Real-World Economic-Cost Evaluation of Physical AI Agents
Keywords: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning
Abstract:
Current navigation benchmarks focus on task success but do not capture the economic constraints essential for commercializing autonomous delivery systems. We introduce CostNav, an Economic Navigation Benchmark that evaluates physical AI agents on a cost-revenue and break-even analysis, pairing Isaac Sim's collision and cargo dynamics with industry-standard data such as Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings and Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) injury reports. To our knowledge, CostNav is the first physics-grounded economic benchmark to use regulatory and financial data to quantify the gap between navigation metrics and commercial deployment, revealing that high task-success rates alone do not ensure economic viability. Evaluating seven baselines (two rule-based and five imitation-learning methods), we find no method economically viable: all yield negative contribution margins. CANVAS, using only an RGB camera and GPS, attains the highest task success and the least-negative margin among methods with non-zero Service-Level Agreement (SLA) compliance (-\28.40/run), outperforming LiDAR-equipped Nav2 w/ GPS (-\37.34/run). A sim-trained policy evaluated on a real delivery robot yields SLA compliance close to its simulation result, indicating that policy performance in CostNav's simulation transfers to real-world deployment. We challenge the community to achieve economic viability on CostNav, which scores methods by cost-revenue outcomes.
PaperID: 606,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Jumman Hossain, Nirmalya Roy
Title: CoGeL: Constraint-to-Geometry Learning from Demonstrations and Failures for Safe Long-Horizon Robot Navigation
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot navigation and locomotion, Robot Learning, Safe Long-Horizon Navigation, Constraint-to-Geometry Learning, Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning, Safety-Aware Quasimetric Learning
Abstract:
Robots are often deployed in environments where safety must be learned from experience rather than specified in advance. Demonstrations, operator interventions, near misses, and failed rollouts can reveal which behaviors are risky, but they provide only local evidence. The key challenge is not only to identify risky behavior, but to make that knowledge shape the distance a robot uses for long-horizon planning. Existing goal-conditioned methods can compose short behaviors into longer plans, but they usually assume the safety-relevant cost is already known. We introduce CoGeL, a constraint-to-geometry learning method that learns a soft safety signal from robot data and incorporates it directly into the goal-reaching distance used for planning. This makes the learned distance safety-aware, instead of treating safety as a separate classifier, hard mask, or post-hoc filter. We show that errors in the learned safety signal lead to controlled changes in the navigation geometry, that approximate distance consistency supports long-horizon composition through waypoints, and that calibrated safety scores limit the expected number of true violations. Experiments across different navigation tasks show that CoGeL substantially reduces unsafe events while preserving strong long-horizon goal-reaching.
PaperID: 607,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Mohammad Omama, Aeyan Ashraf, Sandeep P. Chinchali
Title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Feature-matching, Localization
Abstract:
Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe "interaction bottleneck." Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a lightweight set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, and ETH3D, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.
PaperID: 608,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Chenzhi Liu, Yue Zhang, Jiehong Lin, Jianan Wang, Bo Wang, Zhongrui Wang, Xiaojuan Qi
Title: From Execution to Evolution: A Dual-Loop Agentic System for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
Abstract:
Long-horizon mobile manipulation presents significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and capacity interference between locomotion and arm control. While recent Vision-Language-Action models excel at short-horizon tasks, they lack the hierarchical reasoning required for multi-stage objectives. Furthermore, existing hierarchical agents suffer from rigid sub-task mapping, inflexible replanning, and a lack of continuous learning. To address these limitations, we introduce MobiAgent, a dual-loop agentic framework that bridges robust deployment execution and continuous policy evolution. During deployment, the Inner Loop decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control through highly composable atomic skills. It employs Vision-Language models for receding-horizon planning and visual reflection, dynamically composing skills to ensure robust error recovery. These skills are executed by specialized flow-matching experts that share a unified VLM backbone, maximizing reusability while mitigating capacity interference. Concurrently, the Outer Loop drives automated lifelong learning by autonomously segmenting and verifying deployment rollouts, clustering them to discover atomic skills, and continuously fine-tuning the skill library without human annotations. Evaluations across the simulated BEHAVIOR-1K benchmark and real-world tasks demonstrate that MobiAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art monolithic VLAs, achieving a +22.5% higher success rate in simulation. Furthermore, it demonstrates robust error recovery against critical failures and enables steady, annotation-free policy evolution via autonomous data recycling.
PaperID: 609,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.16444     GitHub
Authors:  Yixue Zhang, Kun Wu, Zhi Gao, Zhen Zhao, Pei Ren, Zhiyuan Xu, Fei Liao, Xinhua Wang, Shichao Fan, Di Wu, Qiuxuan Feng, Meng Li, Zhengping Che, Chang Liu, Jian Tang
Title: RoboGene: Boosting VLA Pre-training via Diversity-Driven Agentic Framework for Real-World Task Generation
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Robotic data generation, Automated Task Generation, VLA Pre-training
Abstract:
The pursuit of general-purpose robotic manipulation is hindered by the scarcity of diverse, real-world interaction data. Unlike the large-scale web vision-language data, robotic data collection is an active process incurring prohibitive physical costs. As a result, the key challenge is not merely to collect more robot data, but to obtain training data that provides informative learning knowledge by broadening behavioral coverage and capturing meaningful variations in objects, scenes, and skills. However, how to automatically curate task proposals that maximize the utility of collected robot data remains a critical yet under-explored challenge. To address this, we introduce RoboGene, an agentic framework designed to automate the generation of diverse and informative manipulation tasks across heterogeneous robotic embodiments, spanning single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. RoboGene integrates three core components: (1) diversity-driven sampling for broad task coverage, (2) agentic self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and (3) human-verified feedback memory for execution-grounded validation and continual refinement. We conduct extensive quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, collecting datasets of 18k trajectories and introducing novel metrics to assess task quality in terms of feasibility and diversity. Results demonstrate that RoboGene significantly outperforms frontier foundation models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Furthermore, real-world experiments show that VLA models trained on data generated by RoboGene achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization, highlighting the importance of high-quality task generation. Our project is available at https://x-robogene.github.io/.
PaperID: 610,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.08735    
Authors:  Jaeho Shin, Maani Ghaffari, Yulun Tian
Title: Learning Adaptive Solvers for Distributed Factor Graph Optimization on Matrix Lie Groups
Keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Learning to optimize, Matrix Lie groups
Abstract:
Modern robotic perception increasingly involves large-scale geometric optimization problems distributed across multiple robots or sessions. However, existing distributed solvers often depend on brittle hand tuning and primarily target rigid body pose graphs. To address this, we present DeepCORD, a learning-augmented framework for distributed factor graph optimization on general matrix Lie groups. By unfolding a parallel and accelerated Riemannian optimizer into differentiable iterations, DeepCORD learns a self-supervised feedback policy that dynamically adapts solver parameters according to the optimization phase and communication status. The resulting method enables adaptive distributed optimization over matrix Lie groups under both synchronous and asynchronous communication regimes. Extensive experiments on real-world \mathrmSE(3) pose graph optimization and \mathrmSL(4) projective submap alignment show that our method achieves lower objective values than existing distributed baselines on most benchmarks across realistic operating scenarios.
PaperID: 611,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Albus Dongchen Fang, Gokul Prabhakaran, Ahmed H Qureshi
Title: Uncertainty-Aware Neural Time Fields for Safe Online Motion Planning in Unknown Environments
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Probabilistic learning and uncertainty in robotics
Abstract:
Safe motion planning during online mapping of unknown environments is critical for autonomous systems operating under limited and noisy perception. Neural Time Fields model arrival time as a learned continuous cost-to-go for motion planning, but existing formulations are typically deterministic and do not account for sensing uncertainty. In particular, Active Neural Time Fields lack mechanisms to ensure safety during online deployment, where limited and noisy observations can degrade the safety of planned trajectories and cause collisions. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware neural time field formulation that models and propagates sensor-induced uncertainty in robot–obstacle distance into arrival-time computation via a risk-sensitive representation. We integrate this formulation into a real-time, closed-loop motion planning framework with chance-constrained trajectory optimization. Experimental results demonstrate reduced collision rates during online navigation while preserving path efficiency compared to deterministic and inflation-based baselines, with additional results demonstrating applicability to manipulator systems.
PaperID: 612,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.12027    
Authors:  Taerim Yoon, Dongho Kang, Kisang Park, Junha Cha, Stelian Coros, Sungjoon Choi
Title: Learning Unions of Convex Sets via Invertible Latent Decomposition for Path Planning
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Robot safety, alignment, and safe learning-based systems, Latent Convex Decomposition, Invertible Neural Networks
Abstract:
Collision-free path planning in cluttered, real-world environments relies on a representation of the collision-free space, and existing representations broadly fall into two categories. Explicit representations, such as unions of convex sets, can be plugged into optimization-based planners as hard collision-free constraints, but their parameters scale poorly with configuration-space dimension. Implicit representations, by contrast, are flexible and scale well to complex geometries, yet typically lack such guarantees. We bridge this gap with ILD (Invertible Latent Decomposition), a framework that jointly learns an invertible mapping and a union of explicit convex polytopes in the resulting latent space. Planning is carried out over these latent convex sets, and the invertible mapping decodes the resulting paths back to the original configuration space while preserving feasibility with respect to the refined explicit safe regions. We further propose Visibility-Guided Sampling (VGS) to keep the convex sets connected for path planning. Across 2D navigation, 6-DoF, and 14-DoF manipulation environments, ILD achieves broader coverage, better inter-set connectivity, and higher path-planning success rates than prior baselines, with zero observed false positives after test-time refinement. On a 14-DoF bimanual manipulator, we further demonstrate real-time collision-free planning, with test-time refinement adapting to scene-geometry changes during real-world deployment on a single 6-DoF arm.
PaperID: 613,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.12402    
Authors:  Jadelynn Dao, Milan Ganai, Yasmina Abukhadra, Ajay Sridhar, Mozhgan Nasr Azadani, Katie Z Luo, Clark Barrett, Jiajun Wu, Chelsea Finn, Marco Pavone
Title: DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Hierarchical Embodied Planning, Test-Time Compute
Abstract:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as high-level planners for embodied agents, with an emerging strategy of scaling test-time compute to improve capability. However, we observe that doing so increases latency, token usage, and FLOPs while yielding uneven, often diminishing gains in downstream success, limiting where embodied agents can be deployed. We argue that choosing when and where to spend test-time compute is central to bringing frontier performance to the real world. We introduce DIRECT, a routing framework that uses multimodal scene context to allocate compute per prompt, improving the success--cost Pareto frontier over fixed model selection. Across three dominant scaling axes, namely chain-of-thought depth, model size, and memory history, our experiments on VLABench and RoboMME show that test-time compute is not a uniform lever: different axes yield qualitatively distinct capability gains. We validate these insights on a physical Franka arm in a DROID setup spanning zero-shot manipulation and long-horizon chaining, where our router matches or exceeds a stronger model's success rate at up to 65% lower average latency. Ultimately, our results show that naively scaling test-time compute is wasteful, and that DIRECT can provide frontier-level embodied planning in robotic systems at a fraction of the cost. Project page can be found at direct-corl.github.io.
PaperID: 614,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.31132    
Authors:  Andrew Zou Li, Gokul Swamy, Yonatan Bisk, Andrea Bajcsy
Title: ELASTIC: Efficiently Learning to Adaptively Scale Test-Time Compute for Generative Control Policies
Keywords: Combination of learning and planning in robotics, Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Test-Time Scaling
Abstract:
Generative control policies (GCPs), such as diffusion policies and flow-based vision-language-action models, enable test-time scaling in robot control. This compute can be allocated along two axes: sequential scaling, which increases denoising steps to refine actions, and parallel scaling, which samples multiple candidate actions to search across modes of the policy distribution. Existing methods typically rely on fixed conservative schedules that may over-compute in easy states and under-allocate in difficult ones. However, the optimal allocation is hard to know a priori as it is state-, task-, and policy-dependent: early stages of a grasp may benefit from broader parallel exploration, while near-contact phases may require more sequential refinement for precision. We present ELASTIC, an algorithm that learns state-dependent test-time compute schedules for GCPs. We formulate compute allocation as a meta-Markov Decision Process in which a meta-policy interacts with a frozen pretrained robot policy and selects sequential steps and parallel samples at each denoising iteration to maximize task success while minimizing compute. Using reinforcement learning, this meta-policy also learns adaptive compute schedules without access to the GCP's training data. Across simulated manipulation benchmarks with diffusion policies, ELASTIC Pareto-dominates fixed and single-axis scaling baselines at matched compute budgets. On real-world robot manipulation with the \pi_0.5 vision-language-action model, ELASTIC matches best-of-10 success while reducing wall-clock latency by 34%.
PaperID: 615,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.14698    
Authors:  Marino Watanabe, Takami Sato, Kentaro Yoshioka
Title: Lights, Camera, Malfunction: When Illumination Robustness Leaves VLA Models Blind to Color
Keywords: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming, Vision-Language-Action Models, Adversarial Robustness
Abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation; however, their transition to real-world environments reveals vulnerabilities to minor environmental perturbations. We propose FLARE, an optimized physical spotlight attack framework that exploits these vulnerabilities via targeted illuminations, dropping baseline task success rates to zero without any access to model internals. While adversarial training is the standard countermeasure, we identify a critical and previously underestimated defensive pitfall: naive data augmentations incorrectly condition VLA models to discard color as noise, collapsing their visual perception into a purely shape-biased processor. We expose this degradation through a diagnostic grayscale evaluation, in which the defended model maintains high success rates on grayscale inputs, while its success rate on benign, color-dependent real-world tasks drops to at most 47.5%, well below the undefended baseline. To address this, we propose ChromaGuard, a chroma-preserving adversarial training method. On a physical 6-DoF robotic platform, we demonstrate that ChromaGuard achieves 97.5% and 92.5% success rates in benign and attacked color-dependent tasks, respectively.
PaperID: 616,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Albert Wilcox, Frank Chang, Nhi Nguyen, Aishani Chakraborty, Jeremy A. Collins, Vaibhav Saxena, Benjamin Joffe, Siddharth Karamcheti, Animesh Garg
Title: MESA: An Evaluation Framework for Compositional, Semantic, and Spatial Generalization in Robotics
Keywords: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems
Abstract:
Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation.
PaperID: 617,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.00915     GitHub
Authors:  Zhiyuan Wu, Xiangyu Zhang, Zhuo Chen, Jiankang Deng, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias, Shan Luo
Title: DiffMorphGrasp: A Diffusion Framework Conditioned on Hand Morphology for Cross-Embodiment Grasp Generation
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Robot grasping, Cross-embodiment
Abstract:
As robots are deployed across diverse environments, manipulation tasks require robot hands with different morphologies to satisfy varying task requirements, hardware capabilities, and cost constraints. However, transferring grasping policies learned on one robot hand to another with a different morphology remains a fundamental challenge due to variations in kinematic structures and degrees of freedom across embodiments. To address these limitations, we propose DiffMorphGrasp, the first diffusion-based framework that incorporates hand morphology-awareness into the generative process for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping that enables zero-shot generalization to unseen robot hand structures. The proposed approach maps grasps from diverse robotic hands into a unified canonical hand representation, providing a common space for learning. Grasp generation is then continuously conditioned on structured representations of hand kinematics, encoded as graphs derived from hand configurations, together with object geometry. In addition, we introduce a loss function that computes joint-level errors over the hand kinematic structure to constrain the generated grasps during training. To evaluate DiffMorphGrasp, we construct a new benchmark for assessing grasp generation performance across robot hands with different morphologies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiffMorphGrasp achieves strong zero-shot generalization to unseen hand morphologies, enabling scalable cross-embodiment grasp deployment.
PaperID: 618,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.13102    
Authors:  Chengbo Yuan, Zicheng Zhang, Mingjie Zhou, Wendi Chen, Yi Wang, Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Shuo Wang, Hui Zhang, Wenkang Zhang, Yingdong Hu, Yuanqing Gong, Wanli Xing, Chuan Wen, Cewu Lu, Kaifeng Zhang, Yang Gao
Title: FTP-1: A Generalist Foundation Tactile Policy Across Tactile Sensors for Contact-Rich Manipulation
Keywords: Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Tactile Manipulation, Generalist Policy
Abstract:
Despite the success of vision-based generalist robotic policies, existing tactile-based policies remain tied to fixed embodiments and sensor setups. This is because tactile signals are highly heterogeneous across hardware, making cross-sensor generalization difficult. We present FTP-1, the first generalist foundation tactile policy pretrained to acquire transferable tactile manipulation abilities across diverse sensors and embodiments. FTP-1 supports varied tactile inputs, including image-, array-, and state-based signals, by using heterogeneous encoders to project them into unified morphology-aware latent tokens that are jointly modeled by a shared tactile Transformer expert. Pretrained on ~ 3,000 hours of tactile manipulation data aggregated from 26 data sources, spanning human and robot demonstrations across 21 sensors, FTP-1 learns tactile skills that transfer beyond the sensors seen during pretraining. Across downstream finetuning experiments spanning 5 hardware configurations, FTP-1 improves contact-rich manipulation on seen sensor setups by +17.2% and, surprisingly, transfers to two previously unseen tactile-sensor setups, achieving a +31% gain in success rate. FTP-1 establishes the first unified foundation baseline for tactile manipulation, providing future tactile policies with a shared model-level starting point. All model checkpoints, datasets, and training code will be released in the future.
PaperID: 619,   Poster  OpenReview   GitHub
Authors:  Hojune Kim, Timothy Chen, Jiankai Sun, Lars Osterberg, Qianzhong Chen, Ke Wang, Mac Schwager
Title: WiGS: Teleop-Free Fine-Tuning of VLAs for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation in a 3DGS Simulator
Keywords: Sim-to-real transfer, Robot foundation models and general-purpose knowledge systems, Humanoid, Vision Language Action Model
Abstract:
Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies for humanoid loco-manipulation is constrained by the high cost and complexity of collecting human teleoperation demonstrations. VLA policies fine-tuned in simulators have so far transferred poorly to humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. We present LEGS (Loco-manipulation via Embodied Gaussian Splatting), a hybrid simulator that composites a mesh foreground (robot, objects, props) over a photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) background reconstructed from a handheld scene capture. LEGS uses a procedural motion-primitive generator to synthesize labeled demonstrations at scale without human teleoperation, and a two-stage color calibration that aligns renders to the deployment camera. On a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, across three pick-and-place tasks of increasing whole-body difficulty and three VLA backbones (psi0, pi0.5, GR00T N1.6), a policy trained purely on LEGS data matches or exceeds one trained on human teleoperation demos on every experiment. It also outperforms a mesh-only baseline trained on the same motions without the calibrated 3DGS frontend. Because motion is recorded independently of appearance, the same demonstrations can be re-rendered for a target scene and objects at over 15x lower cost than teleoperation. When both the objects and the scene change, a policy trained on LEGS-aug data re-rendered for that target maintains task success, while the teleop baseline fails entirely. Code and videos are available at https://hojjunekim.github.io/legs/.
PaperID: 620,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.00641    
Authors:  Yutong Wang, Dongjae Lee, Xiaofeng Guo, Yuanzhu Zhan, Yufei Jiang, Bavin Saravanan, Muqing Cao, Jia Xie, Chenyang Mao, Sebastian Scherer, Junyi Geng, Guanya Shi
Title: AM-Bench: A Modular Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Aerial Manipulation Policy Learning
Keywords: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning, Robot manipulation, Aerial manipulation
Abstract:
Standardized benchmarks such as LIBERO and robosuite have played a central role in advancing robot manipulation learning, yet most focus on ground-supported manipulation systems, limiting their applicability to dynamics-critical domains such as aerial manipulation (AM). This field presents different system-level challenges, including environmental disturbances, coupled dynamics between the manipulator and floating base, and constrained degrees of freedom, causing task performance to depend jointly on robot embodiment, low-level control, and high-level policy design. We introduce AM-Bench, a modular simulation suite and benchmark for multirotor-based AM policy learning. AM-Bench includes representative embodiments spanning fully actuated and underactuated systems, 12 tasks across contact, transport, and constrained interaction, configurable disturbances that reflect real-world effects including aerodynamic effects and actuator saturation, standard low-level controllers, and baseline policy learning algorithms. Unlike prior manipulation benchmarks that primarily emphasize end-to-end policy performance, AM-Bench enables system-level evaluation of how embodiment, control, disturbances, and policy choices interact. We further demonstrate its diagnostic value through benchmark studies that reveal policy performance under AM conditions, different policy--control interface choices, and robot embodiment differences.
PaperID: 621,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Yusen Feng, Bingchen Han, Jiangran Lyu, Kai Liu, Yixin Zheng, Yuxuan Wan, Weiheng Liu, Sun Han, Ruiqin Li, Yulong Zhang, Fangfu Liu, Xuesong Shi, Yizhou Wang, Libin Liu, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
Title: WAM-TTT: Learning to Adapt World-Action Models from Human Play at Test Time
Keywords: Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Scaling generalist manipulation policies is bottlenecked not by model capacity but by teleoperation cost: covering the full distribution of object placements, orientations, and scene contexts that a deployed robot must handle quickly becomes prohibitive. We argue this bottleneck is largely artificial. Human egocentric demonstrations—plentiful, cheap, and naturally diverse—already encode the visual and physical regularities needed to handle out-of-distribution (OOD) configurations; the missing piece is a recipe that injects this knowledge into a robot-specific action head without re-training the embodiment mapping. Building on LDA-1B, a 1B-parameter latent dynamics-action model pretrained jointly on cross-embodiment robot trajectories and human ego video, we propose a post-training recipe that keeps both data sources alive throughout fine-tuning. Specifically, we co-train with five complementary objectives—policy (P), forward dynamics (FD), inverse dynamics (ID), video generation (VG), and joint action-observation denoising (JD)—routed through embodiment-aware heads. Human ego data participates in FD, ID, VG, and JD but is excluded from policy supervision, so it shapes the shared visual-physical representation while leaving the embodiment-specific action head uncontaminated. We further unfreeze the VLM backbone during post-training, recovering cross-embodiment knowledge that a frozen-VLM recipe otherwise abandons. Across rigorous out-of-distribution evaluations and a suite of long-horizon dexterous manipulation tasks on two robot embodiments, our recipe consistently outperforms robot-only baselines and matches policies trained on substantially more teleoperated data—demonstrating that scarce real-robot demonstrations, combined with abundant egocentric human data, are sufficient for strong generalization.
PaperID: 622,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23156    
Authors:  Yueyang Weng, Xiaopeng Zhang, Yuxi Ou, Mu Yongjin, Chengzhi zhao, Yanjie Li
Title: ORD-WM: Learning Object-Centric Rigid Dynamics for 3D World Modeling in Robotic Manipulation
Keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Robot manipulation, 3D Dynamics Prediction
Abstract:
World models provide robots with a predictive mechanism for reasoning about how actions change object states in manipulation tasks. However, existing image-based and dense 3D world models do not explicitly impose object-level rigid motion, leaving rigid-object geometry preservation to be learned implicitly and making multi-step rollouts susceptible to shape drift or object-level motion inconsistency. To address this, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation. ORD-WM learns a vector-neuron variational autoencoder supervised by signed distance fields, which encodes each object point cloud as a geometry-aware latent representation composed of 3D vector features, and uses an action-conditioned dynamics model to predict object-wise SE(3) motion increments. Rather than generating unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM analytically applies predicted object-wise rigid transformations to the current latent states, separating persistent object geometry from pose changes. Experiments show that ORD-WM enables stable, geometry-preserving multi-step prediction and supports efficient real-time replanning for closed-loop model predictive control in simulated and real-world manipulation scenarios. More details and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ORD-WM.
PaperID: 623,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.13977    
Authors:  Zhennan Jiang, Shangqing Zhou, Yutong Jiang, Zefang Huang, Mingjie Wei, YUHUI CHEN, Tianxing Zhou, Zhen Guo, Hao Lin, Quanlu Zhang, Yu Wang, Dongbin Zhao, Haoran Li, Chao Yu
Title: WoVR: World Models as Reliable Simulators for Post-Training VLA Policies with RL
Keywords: Video models and latent world models for robot learning, Model-based and model-free learning for robotic control
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning (RL) promises to unlock capabilities beyond imitation learning for Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models, but its requirement for massive real-world interaction prevents direct deployment on physical robots. Recent work attempts to use learned world models as simulators for policy optimization, yet closed-loop imagined rollouts inevitably suffer from hallucination and long-horizon error accumulation. Such errors not only degrade visual fidelity, but also mislead policy optimization by providing unreliable learning signals. We propose WoVR, a reliable world-model-based RL framework for post-training VLA policies. Instead of assuming a faithful world model, WoVR explicitly regulates how RL interacts with imperfect imagined dynamics. It improves rollout stability through a controllable action-conditioned video world model, reshapes imagined interaction to reduce effective error depth via Keyframe-Initialized Rollouts, and maintains policy--simulator alignment through World Model-Policy co-evolution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WoVR enables stable long-horizon imagined rollouts and effective policy optimization, achieving superior LIBERO performance and consistent real-world gains across multiple robotic platforms. These results show that world models can serve as practical simulators for RL when hallucination is explicitly controlled.
PaperID: 624,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11753    
Authors:  Tengbo Yu, Jiahao Wu, Daohan Li, Bingxu Chen, Hao Liu, Xiaojian Ma, Hangxin Liu
Title: SEED-UMI: Sharing the Exoskeleton between human and robot for onE-to-one Dexterous demonstration
Keywords: Hardware design and optimization, Robot systems, hardware, and sensors for learning
Abstract:
Imitation learning for dexterous hands is bottlenecked by the difficulty of collecting contact-rich demonstrations that transfer faithfully to the robot. Prior wearable-exoskeleton systems record only on the human side and retarget via open-loop mappings calibrated in free space, which degrade under contact. We present SEED-UMI, a framework in which both the human and the robot wear the same exoskeleton: joint encoders become a physically shared measurement, and wrist cameras mounted to the exoskeleton observe the same outer mechanism during both human data collection and robot policy rollouts. This turns retargeting into paired cross-embodiment supervision and lets policies train directly on raw exoskeleton-centric wrist images, without segmentation or inpainting. On five contact-rich tasks, SEED-UMI achieves 3.0× greater data collection efficiency than exoskeleton-based teleoperation and a 70.0% average rollout success rate.
PaperID: 625,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.32236     GitHub GitHub
Authors:  Yu Li, Shenghe Hu, Yuhan Wang, Yaoxiang Pu, Haotong Zhang, Yuanpei Chen, Yaodong Yang
Title: RoboFFT: Finetuning generative robot policy via online reinforcement learning with forward process
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Diffusion RL, Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, have shown strong promise for robot policy learning by capturing complex and multimodal action distributions from demonstrations. However, policies trained solely with imitation learning often suffer from imperfect demonstrations and distributional shifts, while further improvement typically requires additional expert data. Reinforcement learning offers a natural solution through environment interaction, but effectively finetuning generative robot policies remains challenging due to the intractability of likelihood estimation. In this work, we propose RoboFFT, a forward-process reinforcement learning framework for finetuning generative robot policies, which applies forward noising to sampled actions and uses the weighted score / flow matching loss to construct a surrogate policy ratio for PPO-style updates. We evaluate RoboFFT with popular generative robot policy on representative simulation benchmarks, including long-horizon planning and sparse reward settings. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate that RoboFFT consistently improves performance while achieving better stability and training efficiency. We further integrate RoboFFT into a real world RL framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in real world tasks.
PaperID: 626,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.05927    
Authors:  Long Xu, Zhiqi Zhang, Mi Yan, Shengliang Deng, Chong Xia, Mingyu Dong, Jiayi Chen, Jiangran Lyu, Fei Gao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
Title: GIF: Agentic Generation of Interactive and Functional Object Compositions for Robot Learning
Keywords: Robotic data generation, interactive scene generation
Abstract:
Embodied foundation models for manipulation require scalable evaluation and data generation over diverse scenarios, with simulation serving as an important pathway. Automated scene generation offers a promising path, yet prior work has largely emphasized coarse-grained scene layouts rather than fine-grained functional object compositions. Motivated by this gap, we present GIF, an agentic Generation framework for Interactive and Functional object compositions. In this framework, we recast this problem as disentangled reconstruction followed by relative pose recovery. CoGen produces instance-disentangled meshes with coarse initial poses leveraging complementary strengths of 2D and 3D generative models, GPRM refines the relative pose under joint geometric and physical guidance, and a VLM verifier selects the candidate that best matches the structured specification. We further construct a benchmark spanning eight representative contact-geometry classes and compare with state-of-the-art generators; GIF improves both asset quality and relation matching, while reducing collision rate to below 1%. Finally, we synthesize data for policy learning, revealing diversity scaling in both simulation and real-world deployment.
PaperID: 627,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Mrinal Jain, Arpit Gupta, Animesh Garg
Title: An Empirical Study of Data-Loading Bottlenecks (and Non-Bottlenecks) in Robotic Imitation Learning
Keywords: Robot systems, hardware, and sensors for learning, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL)
Abstract:
Modern robotic imitation learning pipelines increasingly rely on large-scale datasets, prompting heavy engineering investments in high-performance data infrastructure under the assumption that dataset loading and online augmentation present primary bottlenecks. We challenge this assumption through a systematic, measurement-driven profile of end-to-end policy training within the LeRobot ecosystem across various spatial resolutions. We evaluate standard implementations against a custom, high-performance Rust data engine utilizing Apache Arrow for zero-copy memory access and a copy-on-write (COW) shared cache. Our profiling reveals three key findings: first, across all reachable configurations on consumer hardware, the data path accounts for a mere 1–4% of per-step training time; second, substantial data-path optimizations yielding massive isolated micro-benchmark speedups translate to zero measurable wall-clock improvement in full training; and third, severe data-path degradation stems solely from format-specific serialization flaws, such as unindexed sequential video decoding. Finally, we argue that future robotics data infrastructure must be evaluated against overall training step ratios rather than isolated benchmarks, shifting the community's optimization paradigm away from data loading and toward upstream model layers like visual feature caching.
PaperID: 628,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Xuanyu Zhang, He Li, Xinxiang Lou, Lu Chen, Yuxiang Cui, Zhongxiang Zhou, Rong Xiong
Title: Anchoring Attention in Clutter: Mask-Guided Latent Distillation for Vision-Language-Action Towards Dexterous Grasping
Keywords: Learning representations for robotic perception and control, Robot manipulation
Abstract:
Dexterous grasping in densely packed same-category clutter remains challenging for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, in part because text-prompted VLAs provide little guidance for selecting among visually identical instances. Although external object masks are commonly provided as visual prompts, making the mask visible does not ensure that the policy maintains focused attention on the masked object---a failure mode especially consequential for dexterous-hand grasping, where small object-grounding errors directly affect contact and closure. We introduce FOCUS, a novel method for Foreground-aware, Object-anchored Continuous grasping that Uses Self-distillation to turn the mask from a passive visual prompt into a training-time alignment signal internalized by the action pathway. During training, FOCUS injects a mask-derived additive bias into the action expert's cross-attention and distills the resulting object-anchored representation into a bias-free pathway, encouraging control to be related to the mask-specified object region rather than object-specific appearance or illumination. To support sequential grasping across multiple objects, a lightweight progress query token co-attends with state and action tokens to trigger sub-task termination and provide phase-aware context. In real-robot experiments at two levels of inter-instance distinguishability, FOCUS achieves 67.5% average grasp success, surpassing all four VLA baselines by at least 26.9 percentage points, with the largest margin (+34.6 points) on the most challenging setting. Additional experiments confirm FOCUS's robustness to unseen object categories (58.4%) and unseen lighting conditions (60.1%), where all four baselines fall below 31%.
PaperID: 629,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.25887     GitHub
Authors:  Ziyan Feng, Zizhao Yuan, Yulong Fu, Yuxin He, Zhiyuan Zhang, Zhengjie Zhang, JINNI ZHOU, Renjing Xu, Qiang Nie
Title: What is the Better Curriculum: Controller-Shaped Grasping Behavior for Contact Force-Sensitive Manipulation
Keywords: Robot manipulation, Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Controller-Shaped Grasping Behavior, Force-Sensitive Manipulation
Abstract:
How should a robot learn to manipulate objects so fragile that sub-Newton contact forces can cause irreversible damage? Prior visuo-tactile policy learning typically treats tactile sensing as an additional modality to integrate into the policy, for example by fusing tactile inputs with vision or using execution-time adaptation. In direct-contact force-sensitive manipulation, however, the main bottleneck arises earlier: during teleoperated data collection, contact force is not directly observable, and visual feedback is too delayed to reliably maintain the narrow force range required for stable grasping. We address this problem with a tactile reflex controller used during collection, producing teleoperated demonstrations with controller-shaped grasping behavior. These shaped demonstrations form a better curriculum for tactile-free policy learning. The effect is clearest on Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), where the learned policy matches the teacher's closing profile and achieves 95% stable grasps on the nominal plastic-cup task. The same data intervention also improves in-distribution stability and transfer to an unseen paper-cup variant on π₀.₅. Under randomized external disturbance, however, the same reflex-data π₀.₅ policy fails in 45% of policy-only trials, whereas deterministic reflex arbitration preserves the grasp with no failures. These results reveal a new role for tactile feedback in force-sensitive manipulation: rather than integrating tactile into the policy, we use it as a collection-time teacher that shapes grasping behavior in demonstrations for policy learning, while disturbance rejection remains controller-dependent, revealing the boundary of tactile-free policy.
PaperID: 630,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Nicklas Sohm, Aswin Ramachandran, Raffaello D'Andrea
Title: KlaskTron-IL: A Contact-Rich Adversarial Imitation Learning Benchmark with a Validated Sim-to-Real Bridge
Keywords: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning, Imitation learning (behavioral cloning, inverse RL), Adversarial multi-agent imitation learning, Sim-to-real transfer
Abstract:
KlaskTron is an open-hardware physical platform for two-player adversarial reinforcement learning, with a learned actuator model that supports zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of trained policies. Building on this platform, we contribute KlaskTron-IL: a multi-tier imitation learning dataset (80k human demonstration timesteps collected directly on the physical robot, 320k symmetry-augmented timesteps, and synthetic expert trajectories up to 5M steps generated by the zero-shot-validated PPO policy), a GPU-native Isaac Lab environment, and diagnostic baselines that expose three characteristic failure modes of standard IL methods under contact-rich adversarial dynamics: BC's data scaling plateau, GAIL's interpretable but unusable discriminator (Spearman \rho = -1.0 peg--ball proximity recovery with a logit gradient too flat to drive PPO), and an asymmetric BC-prior × reward-density interaction. Because the policy interface used throughout this paper is the same one the actuator model bridges to hardware, algorithms developed against these diagnostics are immediately deployable on the physical robot.
PaperID: 631,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Jiwei Sun, Jingyu XU, Zhuang Zhang, Ronghua Hu, Xingxing Zhang, Hua Yang
Title: Damage-Aware Quadruped Locomotion: Zero-Shot Adaptation to Motor Failures via Pain-Inspired Reinforcement Learning
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Fault-tolerant legged locomotion, Quadruped robots
Abstract:
Quadruped robots are expected to operate reliably in dynamic and unstructured environments, where unexpected motor failures may occur and severely degrade locomotion performance. Traditional fault-tolerant control methods typically rely on explicit fault detection or handcrafted recovery strategies, which limit their responsiveness and generalization. In this work, we present a damage-aware adaptive control framework that enables quadruped robots to achieve zero-shot locomotion adaptation under sudden motor failures. At its core lies a pain-inspired reinforcement learning paradigm in which the reward explicitly constrains policy behavior, forcing the robot to exploit actuator-health cues from the ontology-sense module, and thereby promoting safer, more protective responses to faults. To improve robustness, we design a failure-probability curriculum that gradually increases the chance of motor failures during training. Evaluations under weakened-motor and locked-joint faults show that the resulting policy achieves lower velocity-tracking errors than SOTA reference across all evaluated fault categories. Comprehensive experiments in both the high-fidelity Isaac Gym simulator and real quadruped hardware demonstrate that our framework achieves robust, damage-aware locomotion, marking a step toward resilient and deployable fault-tolerant legged robots.
PaperID: 632,   Poster  OpenReview  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.27366    
Authors:  Lijin Yang, Zhongzhan Huang, Jianing Huang, Shu Liu, Hao Yang
Title: Judge, Then Drive: A Critic-Centric Vision Language Action Framework for Autonomous Driving
Keywords: Autonomous driving and flight
Abstract:
Recent advances in vision language action (VLA) models have shown remarkable potential for autonomous driving by directly mapping multimodal inputs to control signals. However, previous VLA-based methods have not explicitly exploited the critic capability of VLAs to refine driving decisions, even though such capability has been well demonstrated in other LLM-based domains, thereby limiting their performance in complex closed-loop scenarios. In this work, we present a theoretically inspired two-stage framework, CriticVLA, which extends the role of VLAs from acting to judging. CriticVLA first generates a rough trajectory and then refines it through multimodal evaluation and single-step optimization guided by a VLA-based critic, yielding higher-quality driving behaviors. To support this process, we construct a large-scale synthetic dataset of 12.9 million annotated trajectories covering diverse driving scenarios, which enhances the critic’s reasoning and refinement abilities. Extensive closed-loop experiments on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that CriticVLA significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a 73.33% total success rate and delivering about 30% improvement in challenging scenarios.
PaperID: 633,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Luca Benfenati, Ali Azimi, Matteo Risso, Fabio Carapellese, Daniele Jahier Pagliari, Alessio Burrello
Title: Before Parc Fermé: RL-Time Pruning for Efficient Embodied LLMs in Autonomous Driving
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Autonomous driving and flight, Large Language Models, Training-Time Pruning
Abstract:
Embodied Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning modules in robotic control pipelines to improve human-robot interaction, but their memory and generation latency make real-time deployment difficult. Pruning can reduce these costs, but for controllers that undergo multiple pre- and post-training phases, the crucial question is not only how much to prune, but when pruning should occur. In this work, we propose Before Parc Fermé (BPF), a pruning strategy performed during RL that compresses embodied LLM controllers while they are still being optimized for closed-loop behavior. This allows pruning decisions to account for the task-specific supervision and closed-loop feedback that shape the final controller. We propose two variants: BPF-RL, which performs iterative pruning during RL by removing part of the model at predefined training intervals, and BPF-SFT/RL, which first prunes part of the model structure during SFT and then further compresses it during RL using the same iterative strategy as BPF-RL until the target pruning ratio is reached. We evaluate BPF on RobotxR1, an LLM-based autonomous-driving control pipeline, using an established LLM pruning framework (LLM-Pruner), and compare it against post-training pruning, post-training pruning with RL recovery, SFT-stage pruning, and smaller dense models from the same family. Our results show that BPF provides the best task-performance vs. memory and throughput trade-off among the considered pruning strategies. When compressing the larger RobotxR1 models, BPF-SFT/RL achieves a 1.69× better size-end-to-end performance trade-off than directly selecting a smaller dense model from the same family, measured as removed parameters per lost percentage point of control adaptability. On the Jetson AGX Orin mounted on the target robotic platform, the compact models improve decode throughput by up to 27%. Finally,we further show that pruning must be evaluated end-to-end, since changes in generated output tokens can affect downstream latency and closed-loop behavior.
PaperID: 634,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Shengtao Wu, Zichao Dong, Weixuan Qiao, Xiaolu Liu, Xin Zhan, Junbo Chen, Jianke Zhu
Title: From Foundation VLM to Versatile Driving VLM: A Triplet Incremental Training Approach
Keywords: Multimodal perception, sensor fusion, and robot vision, Autonomous driving and flight
Abstract:
Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. This insight reveals that instead of complex over-engineering, general VLMs merely require a targeted geometric catalyst to bridge the spatial gap. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.
PaperID: 635,   Poster  OpenReview  
Authors:  Pengzhi Yang, Xinyu Wang, Pengyu Jing, Kehan Wen, Yiduo Qu, Zhenhao Huang, Minghao Fu, Xin Liu, Yaheng Shen, Fan Shi
Title: Progress That Trains: Reference-Anchored Reward Modeling for Robotic Manipulation from a Single Demonstration
Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Robot manipulation, Reward Model
Abstract:
Reinforcement learning for robot manipulation is bottlenecked by reward design: hand-crafted rewards are brittle and prohibitively task-specific, while learned reward models typically demand additional task data and handle failures poorly, leaving them vulnerable to reward hacking. To address this, we introduce the Reference-Anchored Reward Model (RARM), a lightweight visual comparator that leverages a single reference demonstration to generate dense, progress-aware rewards with no per-task reward engineering. RARM couples a DINOv3 backbone with low-rank adapters, a temporal aggregator, and an asymmetric cross-attention comparator, trained once with a contrastive objective on ordinary videos and requiring no robot-specific data. At policy-training time, each rollout clip is matched against reference clips from the demonstration, and the reward is based on confidence-gated progress change from the matched clip, anchoring learning to that single demonstration. Across 10 simulated tasks (LIBERO, MetaWorld) and 4 real-world tasks, including long-horizon settings, RARM achieves the best overall success rates while adding negligible per-step reward generation overhead.
